title: Systematic approach to reading a 12-lead ECG
summary: A reproducible, sequential method for interpreting any 12-lead ECG. Reading every trace in the same order (rate, rhythm, axis, intervals, then morphology) reduces missed findings. Always interpret in the context of the patient and compare with prior ECGs where available.

steps.detail: Check patient name, date/time and that paper speed is 25 mm/s and calibration is 10 mm/mV. At 25 mm/s each small (1 mm) square = 0.04 s and each large (5 mm) square = 0.20 s.
If regular, 300 divided by the number of large squares between R waves, or count QRS complexes in a 10-second rule-of-300/6-second strip x 10 if irregular. Normal resting rate 60-100/min.
Is it regular or irregular? Is there a P wave before every QRS and a QRS after every P? Are P waves uniform and upright in II? Establish sinus vs non-sinus.
Look at leads I and aVF. Normal axis: QRS positive in both I and aVF (-30 to +90 degrees). Left axis deviation: positive I, negative aVF. Right axis deviation: negative I, positive aVF.
PR 120-200 ms (3-5 small squares); QRS <120 ms (<3 small squares); QT corrected for rate (see long QT entry).
Assess P-wave, QRS (Q waves, R-wave progression, hypertrophy), ST segments (elevation/depression), T waves and U waves systematically lead by lead and by territory.

sections.heading: Lead groupings by territory
items: Inferior: II, III, aVF (right coronary artery, sometimes left circumflex)
Septal: V1-V2 (left anterior descending)
Anterior: V3-V4 (left anterior descending)
Lateral: I, aVL, V5-V6 (left circumflex / diagonal)
Reciprocal change in opposite leads supports a true ischaemic event

references.label: AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for the Standardization and Interpretation of the Electrocardiogram (Circulation 2007)

title: Normal ECG intervals and reference values
summary: Reference values for the standard ECG intervals and durations at a paper speed of 25 mm/s. These provide the baseline against which abnormalities (block, pre-excitation, prolongation) are judged.

sections.heading: Reference values
items: Paper speed 25 mm/s: 1 small square (1 mm) = 0.04 s; 1 large square (5 mm) = 0.20 s
Heart rate (normal resting): 60-100 beats/min
P-wave duration: <120 ms (<3 small squares); amplitude <2.5 mm in II
PR interval: 120-200 ms (3-5 small squares)
QRS duration: <120 ms (<3 small squares); 110-120 ms is borderline
QT interval: rate-dependent; corrected QT (QTc) normally <=440 ms (men) and <=460 ms (women)
QRS axis: -30 to +90 degrees is normal

references.label: AHA/ACCF/HRS Standardization and Interpretation of the ECG Part IV: ST/T/QT (Circulation 2009)

title: ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) - recognition by territory
summary: STEMI is identified by new ST-segment elevation at the J point in two contiguous leads exceeding sex/age and lead-specific thresholds, usually with reciprocal ST depression. It mandates immediate reperfusion (primary PCI or fibrinolysis). Localising the territory predicts the culprit artery and complications.

sections.heading: Diagnostic ST-elevation thresholds (new, at J point, in 2 contiguous leads)
items: Leads other than V2-V3: >=1 mm (0.1 mV) elevation in all such leads
V2-V3 in men >=40 years: >=2 mm (0.2 mV)
V2-V3 in men <40 years: >=2.5 mm (0.25 mV)
V2-V3 in women (any age): >=1.5 mm (0.15 mV)
New (or presumed new) LBBB with strongly ischaemic symptoms is managed as STEMI-equivalent

sections.heading: Territory localisation and likely culprit
items: Inferior (II, III, aVF) -> right coronary artery (or left circumflex); consider right-sided leads for RV infarct
Anteroseptal (V1-V4) -> left anterior descending
Anterolateral (V3-V6, I, aVL) -> LAD / left circumflex / diagonal
Lateral (I, aVL, V5-V6) -> left circumflex / diagonal
Posterior (tall R and ST depression V1-V3, ST elevation in posterior leads V7-V9) -> left circumflex / RCA

redFlags: ST elevation meeting threshold in 2 contiguous leads -> activate primary PCI / reperfusion pathway immediately
Inferior STEMI with hypotension -> obtain right-sided leads (V4R) for RV infarction; avoid nitrates
New LBBB with ischaemic symptoms -> treat as STEMI-equivalent

references.label: 2023 ESC Guidelines for the management of acute coronary syndromes (Eur Heart J)
Fourth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction (2018)

title: NSTEMI / myocardial ischaemia on ECG
summary: Non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome shows ischaemic ECG changes without persistent diagnostic ST elevation. The ECG may be normal; diagnosis relies on serial ECGs, troponin and the clinical picture. Dynamic or new changes carry the most weight.

sections.heading: Key findings
items: Horizontal or downsloping ST depression >=0.5 mm in 2 contiguous leads -> ischaemia
T-wave inversion >=1 mm in leads with dominant R wave -> ischaemia (consider Wellens pattern in V2-V3 suggesting critical LAD stenosis)
Transient ST elevation that resolves -> unstable angina / vasospasm
A normal ECG does not exclude NSTEMI; perform serial ECGs and serial high-sensitivity troponin
ST depression maximal in V1-V3 with tall R may indicate posterior STEMI rather than NSTEMI

redFlags: Dynamic ST depression with ongoing pain or haemodynamic instability -> high-risk NSTE-ACS, urgent (<24 h or immediate) invasive strategy
ST depression >=8 leads plus aVR elevation -> consider left main / triple-vessel disease

references.label: 2023 ESC Guidelines for the management of acute coronary syndromes (Eur Heart J)

title: Hyperkalaemia on ECG
summary: Hyperkalaemia produces a progressive sequence of ECG changes that broadly correlate with severity but are not reliable enough to exclude dangerous hyperkalaemia. Any ECG change in a patient with known/suspected hyperkalaemia is an emergency requiring membrane stabilisation with calcium.

sections.heading: Progression of changes (roughly by rising K+)

steps.detail: Tall, peaked, narrow-based, symmetrical T waves; shortened QT.
P-wave flattening/widening then loss of P waves; PR prolongation; progressive QRS widening.
Markedly broad QRS merging with T to form a sine-wave pattern; bradycardia; risk of VF or asystole.

redFlags: Any ECG change attributable to hyperkalaemia (peaked T, wide QRS, loss of P, sine wave) -> give IV calcium for cardiac protection immediately, then treatments to shift and remove potassium
Sine-wave QRS or bradyarrhythmia -> peri-arrest, treat without waiting for confirmatory potassium

references.label: Resuscitation Council UK - Emergency treatment of hyperkalaemia (2023)

title: Hypokalaemia on ECG
summary: Low serum potassium prolongs repolarisation and predisposes to ventricular arrhythmia, particularly when combined with other QT-prolonging factors or hypomagnesaemia. ECG changes are not sensitive and severity should be judged on measured potassium.

sections.heading: Key findings
items: Flattened or inverted T waves
Prominent U waves (best seen V2-V3), which may fuse with T to give apparent long QT (true QU prolongation)
ST-segment depression
With severe depletion: increased P-wave amplitude, PR prolongation and increased ventricular ectopy

redFlags: Prolonged QU with ventricular ectopy -> risk of torsades de pointes; correct potassium and magnesium
Hypokalaemia in a patient on digoxin -> markedly increased risk of digoxin toxicity and arrhythmia

references.label: AHA/ACCF/HRS Standardization and Interpretation of the ECG Part IV (Circulation 2009)

title: Atrial fibrillation on ECG
summary: Atrial fibrillation is the commonest sustained arrhythmia, characterised by disorganised atrial activity with an irregularly irregular ventricular response. Recognition matters for rate/rhythm control and, critically, stroke-prevention anticoagulation decisions.

sections.heading: Key findings
items: Irregularly irregular R-R intervals -> hallmark of AF
Absence of distinct, consistent P waves
Fibrillatory (f) waves: chaotic baseline, best seen in V1
Narrow QRS unless pre-existing or rate-related aberrancy/bundle branch block
Ventricular rate often >100/min when uncontrolled (fast AF)

redFlags: AF with rapid rate and haemodynamic instability (shock, ischaemia, heart failure, syncope) -> emergency synchronised cardioversion
Irregular broad-complex tachycardia with very fast rates (>200-250/min) and varying QRS -> consider AF with pre-excitation (WPW); avoid AV-nodal blocking drugs

references.label: 2024 ESC Guidelines for the management of atrial fibrillation (Eur Heart J)

title: Atrial flutter on ECG
summary: Atrial flutter is a macro-reentrant atrial tachycardia, typically with an atrial rate around 300/min. The classic sawtooth flutter waves and rates that are simple fractions of 300 (150, 100, 75) help distinguish it from other tachycardias.

sections.heading: Key findings
items: Sawtooth flutter (F) waves, classically negative in II, III, aVF (typical counterclockwise isthmus-dependent flutter)
Atrial rate approximately 250-350/min (often ~300/min)
Regular ventricular rate that is a fraction of the atrial rate: 2:1 block gives ~150/min, 3:1 gives ~100/min, 4:1 gives ~75/min
A regular narrow-complex tachycardia at exactly ~150/min should prompt suspicion of 2:1 atrial flutter

redFlags: Flutter with 1:1 conduction (rate ~300/min) -> haemodynamic compromise, urgent cardioversion
Flutter with instability -> synchronised cardioversion; anticoagulation considerations mirror those for AF

references.label: 2019 ESC Guidelines for supraventricular tachycardia (Eur Heart J)

title: Supraventricular tachycardia (regular narrow-complex)
summary: Paroxysmal SVT (most commonly AVNRT or AVRT) presents as a regular narrow-complex tachycardia, usually 150-250/min, often with no visible or retrograde P waves. Vagal manoeuvres and adenosine are both diagnostic and therapeutic in the stable patient.

sections.heading: Key findings
items: Regular, narrow QRS (<120 ms) tachycardia, typically 150-250/min
P waves often absent, buried in QRS, or seen as retrograde (pseudo-R' in V1 / pseudo-S in inferior leads) in AVNRT
Abrupt onset and termination
Broad QRS during SVT suggests aberrant conduction or pre-excitation - treat broad-complex tachycardia as VT until proven otherwise

redFlags: SVT with instability (hypotension, ischaemia, heart failure, reduced consciousness) -> immediate synchronised cardioversion
Do not assume a broad-complex regular tachycardia is SVT with aberrancy - default to treating as VT unless a clear prior diagnosis exists

references.label: 2019 ESC Guidelines for supraventricular tachycardia (Eur Heart J)
Resuscitation Council UK - Adult tachycardia algorithm (2021)

title: Ventricular tachycardia (VT) on ECG
summary: VT is a broad-complex tachycardia originating below the AV node and is a life-threatening emergency. Any regular broad-complex tachycardia should be treated as VT unless there is clear evidence of an alternative supraventricular cause.

sections.heading: Key findings
items: Broad QRS (>=120 ms) tachycardia, regular, usually >100/min (commonly 120-250/min)
AV dissociation (independent P waves), capture beats and fusion beats strongly favour VT
Very broad QRS (>160 ms), extreme axis, and concordance across precordial leads favour VT
Monomorphic VT: uniform QRS morphology; polymorphic VT: beat-to-beat changing morphology (consider torsades if long QT)

redFlags: Pulseless VT -> cardiac arrest; immediate defibrillation and CPR
VT with a pulse and instability -> synchronised cardioversion
Polymorphic VT with long QT (torsades) -> IV magnesium and correct precipitants

references.label: Resuscitation Council UK - Adult Advanced Life Support guidelines (2021)
2022 ESC Guidelines for ventricular arrhythmias and prevention of sudden cardiac death (Eur Heart J)

title: Ventricular fibrillation (VF) on ECG
summary: VF is chaotic, disorganised ventricular electrical activity producing no effective cardiac output. It is a shockable cardiac arrest rhythm requiring immediate defibrillation and CPR.

sections.heading: Key findings
items: Chaotic, irregular waveform with no identifiable P waves, QRS complexes or T waves
Variable amplitude and frequency (coarse vs fine VF)
No organised rhythm; patient is pulseless
Exclude artefact (movement, loose leads) only if the patient is conscious with a pulse - never delay treatment of true VF

redFlags: VF on the monitor in a pulseless patient -> immediate defibrillation, high-quality CPR, follow ALS algorithm

references.label: Resuscitation Council UK - Adult Advanced Life Support guidelines (2021)

title: Atrioventricular (heart) block - first, second and third degree
summary: AV block describes impaired conduction between atria and ventricles, graded by severity. Distinguishing the type matters because Mobitz II and complete (third-degree) block carry a high risk of asystole and usually require pacing.

steps.detail: PR interval prolonged >200 ms (>1 large square), constant, with every P conducted. Usually benign.
Progressive PR lengthening until a P wave fails to conduct (dropped QRS), then the cycle repeats. Often benign.
Constant PR interval with intermittent non-conducted P waves (dropped QRS) without prior PR lengthening. High risk of progression to complete block.
Complete AV dissociation: P waves and QRS complexes are independent, with a slower escape rhythm (narrow junctional or broad ventricular).

redFlags: Mobitz II or complete heart block -> high risk of asystole; urgent cardiology/pacing referral and consider transcutaneous pacing
Any AV block with bradycardia and adverse signs (shock, syncope, heart failure, myocardial ischaemia) -> follow bradycardia algorithm (atropine, then pacing)

references.label: 2021 ESC Guidelines on cardiac pacing and cardiac resynchronization therapy (Eur Heart J)
Resuscitation Council UK - Adult bradycardia algorithm (2021)

title: Left bundle branch block (LBBB)
summary: LBBB widens the QRS due to delayed left ventricular activation. New LBBB with ischaemic symptoms is a STEMI-equivalent, and the abnormal repolarisation makes standard ST-segment interpretation unreliable (Sgarbossa criteria are used instead).

sections.heading: Key findings
items: Broad QRS >=120 ms
Dominant S wave in V1 (QS or rS pattern)
Broad, notched ('M-shaped') monophasic R wave in lateral leads (I, aVL, V5-V6) with absent septal Q waves
Appropriate (discordant) ST/T changes opposite to the main QRS deflection - do not read these as primary ischaemia
Use Sgarbossa criteria to identify acute MI in the presence of LBBB

redFlags: New (or presumed new) LBBB with symptoms of myocardial ischaemia -> treat as STEMI-equivalent and activate reperfusion pathway
Concordant ST elevation/depression or excessively discordant ST elevation (Sgarbossa) -> acute MI

references.label: AHA/ACCF/HRS Standardization and Interpretation of the ECG Part III: Intraventricular Conduction (Circulation 2009)

title: Right bundle branch block (RBBB)
summary: RBBB delays right ventricular activation, widening the QRS with a characteristic terminal pattern. Unlike LBBB, RBBB does not by itself preclude interpretation of left-sided ST changes, but new RBBB can accompany acute LAD occlusion or PE.

sections.heading: Key findings
items: Broad QRS >=120 ms
RSR' ('M-shaped' / 'rabbit ears') pattern in V1-V2
Wide, slurred S wave in lateral leads I, aVL, V5-V6
Appropriate discordant ST/T changes (T-wave inversion) in the right precordial leads V1-V3
Incomplete RBBB: same morphology with QRS 110-120 ms

redFlags: New RBBB with ischaemic symptoms can accompany proximal LAD occlusion - interpret with the clinical picture and troponin
New RBBB with right heart strain features may indicate acute pulmonary embolism

references.label: AHA/ACCF/HRS Standardization and Interpretation of the ECG Part III: Intraventricular Conduction (Circulation 2009)

title: Left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) on ECG
summary: ECG criteria estimate increased LV muscle mass by QRS voltage and associated repolarisation changes. The ECG is specific but insensitive; echocardiography is the reference standard. The Sokolow-Lyon and Cornell voltage criteria are the most widely cited.

sections.heading: Voltage criteria
items: Sokolow-Lyon: S wave in V1 + R wave in V5 or V6 >=35 mm; or R in aVL >=11 mm
Cornell voltage: R in aVL + S in V3 >28 mm (men) or >20 mm (women)
Associated 'strain' pattern: down-sloping ST depression and T-wave inversion in lateral leads (I, aVL, V5-V6)
Left axis deviation and broad notched P (left atrial enlargement) may accompany LVH
Voltage criteria overestimate LVH in thin/young patients and underestimate it in obesity/COPD

references.label: AHA/ACCF/HRS Standardization and Interpretation of the ECG Part V: Chamber Hypertrophy (Circulation 2009)

title: Long QT interval on ECG
summary: A prolonged corrected QT (QTc) reflects delayed ventricular repolarisation and predisposes to torsades de pointes. Causes include drugs, electrolyte disturbance (low K+, Mg2+, Ca2+) and congenital long-QT syndromes. Measure QT and correct for rate (e.g. Bazett: QTc = QT / square root of RR in seconds).

sections.heading: Thresholds and assessment
items: Normal QTc: <=440 ms (men), <=460 ms (women)
Borderline: 440/460-499 ms
Prolonged / high risk: QTc >=500 ms, or any acute increase >60 ms from baseline
Measure QT in lead II or V5-V6, from QRS onset to T-wave end; correct for heart rate (Bazett formula commonly used; less accurate at rate extremes)
Look for and correct hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypocalcaemia and review QT-prolonging drugs

redFlags: QTc >=500 ms or rapid prolongation -> high risk of torsades de pointes; stop offending drugs and correct electrolytes
Torsades de pointes (polymorphic VT with long QT) -> IV magnesium sulphate

references.label: AHA/ACCF/HRS Standardization and Interpretation of the ECG Part IV: ST/T/QT (Circulation 2009)

title: Acute pericarditis on ECG
summary: Acute pericarditis produces widespread (non-territorial) ST elevation and PR depression from epicardial inflammation. The key bedside task is distinguishing it from STEMI, where ST elevation is territorial with reciprocal change.

sections.heading: Key findings
items: Widespread concave ('saddle-shaped') ST elevation across multiple, non-contiguous territories
PR-segment depression (and PR elevation in aVR) - a useful supportive sign
No reciprocal ST depression except in aVR (and sometimes V1)
Spodick's sign: down-sloping TP segment may be seen
Evolves through stages; later diffuse T-wave inversion

sections.heading: Distinguishing from STEMI
items: STEMI: ST elevation in a coronary territory with reciprocal depression; pericarditis: diffuse, no reciprocal change
PR depression favours pericarditis; convex ('tombstone') ST elevation favours STEMI
If in doubt, treat the higher-risk diagnosis (STEMI) and seek urgent cardiology input

redFlags: Do not mislabel a STEMI as pericarditis - territorial ST elevation with reciprocal change mandates urgent reperfusion assessment
Pericarditis with effusion and haemodynamic compromise -> consider cardiac tamponade

references.label: 2015 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of pericardial diseases (Eur Heart J)

title: Pulmonary embolism / right heart strain on ECG
summary: The ECG in PE is neither sensitive nor specific; sinus tachycardia is the commonest finding. ECG signs of acute right heart strain support the diagnosis but a normal ECG does not exclude PE - use a validated pre-test probability score and definitive imaging.

sections.heading: Key findings
items: Sinus tachycardia - the most common finding
S1Q3T3 pattern: S wave in lead I, Q wave and T-wave inversion in lead III (classic but uncommon and non-specific)
T-wave inversion in right precordial leads V1-V3 (right ventricular strain) and inferior leads
New incomplete or complete RBBB
Right axis deviation; signs of right atrial enlargement (P pulmonale)

redFlags: ECG signs of right heart strain with hypotension -> consider massive/high-risk PE and obstructive shock
A normal ECG never excludes PE - rely on pre-test probability (e.g. Wells) and CTPA/V-Q imaging

references.label: 2019 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of acute pulmonary embolism (Eur Heart J)

title: Digoxin effect and toxicity on ECG
summary: Therapeutic digoxin produces characteristic repolarisation changes ('digoxin effect') that are not in themselves toxic. Digoxin toxicity, by contrast, causes a wide range of arrhythmias and is potentiated by hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and renal impairment.

sections.heading: Digoxin effect (therapeutic)
items: Down-sloping ST depression with a 'reverse tick' / 'Salvador Dali moustache' appearance
Flattened, inverted or biphasic T waves
Shortened QT interval
Slightly prolonged PR interval (increased vagal tone)

sections.heading: Digoxin toxicity (any arrhythmia possible)
items: Increased automaticity with impaired conduction is characteristic (e.g. atrial tachycardia with AV block)
Frequent ventricular ectopy, bigeminy
Bradyarrhythmias and varying degrees of AV block
Bidirectional VT is highly suggestive of digoxin toxicity

redFlags: Life-threatening dysrhythmia or significant bradyarrhythmia with digoxin toxicity -> consider digoxin-specific antibody fragments (DigiFab)
Hyperkalaemia in acute digoxin toxicity is a marker of severity

references.label: AHA/ACCF/HRS Standardization and Interpretation of the ECG Part IV: ST/T/QT (Circulation 2009)

title: Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) pre-excitation
summary: WPW pattern reflects an accessory pathway that pre-excites the ventricle, producing a short PR and a delta wave. The danger is pre-excited atrial fibrillation, where AV-nodal blocking drugs can accelerate conduction down the accessory pathway and precipitate VF.

sections.heading: Key findings
items: Short PR interval <120 ms
Delta wave: slurred upstroke of the QRS
Widened QRS >110-120 ms
Secondary ST/T changes
AVRT (orthodromic) gives a regular narrow-complex tachycardia; pre-excited AF gives an irregular broad-complex tachycardia with varying QRS

redFlags: Irregular, fast, broad-complex tachycardia with varying QRS -> suspect pre-excited AF; AVOID AV-nodal blockers (adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, beta-blockers, digoxin)
Pre-excited AF with instability -> synchronised cardioversion

references.label: 2019 ESC Guidelines for supraventricular tachycardia (Eur Heart J)

title: Systematic interpretation of arterial/venous blood gas
summary: A stepwise method to classify any acid-base disturbance. Reading the pH, then CO2 and HCO3 in a fixed order, identifies the primary disorder, whether compensation is appropriate, and whether more than one disorder coexists. Always interpret alongside the clinical picture.

steps.detail: Look at PaO2 and SpO2 with the inspired oxygen. Hypoxaemia (PaO2 <8 kPa / 60 mmHg on air) defines respiratory failure; combined with raised CO2 it is type 2.

steps.step: Is the pH acidaemic or alkalaemic?
steps.detail: Normal arterial pH 7.35-7.45. pH <7.35 = acidaemia; pH >7.45 = alkalaemia. This sets the direction of the primary process.
Normal PaCO2 4.7-6.0 kPa (35-45 mmHg). A high CO2 with low pH = respiratory acidosis; a low CO2 with high pH = respiratory alkalosis.

steps.step: Look at the HCO3 / base excess (metabolic component)
steps.detail: Normal HCO3 22-26 mmol/L. Low HCO3 with low pH = metabolic acidosis; high HCO3 with high pH = metabolic alkalosis.
The component (CO2 or HCO3) that has changed in the same direction as the pH abnormality is the primary disorder.
Apply expected-compensation rules (e.g. Winter's formula for metabolic acidosis). If compensation is outside the expected range, or both components shift pH the same way, a mixed disorder is present.
In metabolic acidosis, compute the anion gap (and correct for albumin) to separate raised-gap from normal-gap causes.

references.label: Merck Manual Professional - Acid-Base Regulation and Disorders

title: Respiratory acidosis
summary: Respiratory acidosis is a primary rise in PaCO2 (alveolar hypoventilation) producing acidaemia. Distinguishing acute from chronic depends on the degree of renal (bicarbonate) compensation, which takes 3-5 days to develop fully.

sections.heading: Key findings and compensation
items: Primary disorder: PaCO2 >6.0 kPa (>45 mmHg) with pH <7.35
Acute: HCO3 rises ~1 mmol/L for every 10 mmHg (1.33 kPa) rise in PaCO2
Chronic (renal compensation, 3-5 days): HCO3 rises ~3.5-4 mmol/L for every 10 mmHg rise in PaCO2
Causes: COPD, neuromuscular weakness, opioid/sedative overdose, chest wall disease, airway obstruction, reduced respiratory drive

redFlags: Acute severe respiratory acidosis with falling conscious level -> impending respiratory arrest; consider ventilatory support
Rising CO2 with declining pH despite oxygen therapy in COPD -> reassess oxygen target and need for NIV

references.label: Merck Manual Professional - Respiratory Acidosis

title: Respiratory alkalosis
summary: Respiratory alkalosis is a primary fall in PaCO2 (alveolar hyperventilation) producing alkalaemia. It is common and often reflects an underlying problem (hypoxia, sepsis, PE, anxiety, salicylate toxicity) that must be identified.

sections.heading: Key findings and compensation
items: Primary disorder: PaCO2 <4.7 kPa (<35 mmHg) with pH >7.45
Acute: HCO3 falls ~2 mmol/L for every 10 mmHg (1.33 kPa) fall in PaCO2
Chronic: HCO3 falls ~4-5 mmol/L for every 10 mmHg fall in PaCO2
Causes: hypoxaemia, pain/anxiety, sepsis, pulmonary embolism, pregnancy, salicylate toxicity (early), CNS disease, excessive mechanical ventilation

redFlags: Respiratory alkalosis with hypoxaemia -> look for PE or another serious pulmonary cause rather than attributing to anxiety
Mixed respiratory alkalosis and raised-gap metabolic acidosis -> consider salicylate poisoning

references.label: Merck Manual Professional - Respiratory Alkalosis

title: Metabolic acidosis - raised vs normal anion gap
summary: Metabolic acidosis is a primary fall in bicarbonate. Calculating the anion gap separates the differential into raised-anion-gap (added acid) and normal-anion-gap (hyperchloraemic, bicarbonate loss) causes, which guides the search for a cause.

steps.detail: pH <7.35 with HCO3 <22 mmol/L. Expect compensatory respiratory drop in CO2.
Anion gap = Na - (Cl + HCO3); normal ~8-12 mmol/L. Correct for albumin: add ~2.5 mmol/L to the gap for every 10 g/L the albumin is below 40 g/L.
Lactic acidosis, ketoacidosis (diabetic/alcoholic/starvation), renal failure (uraemia), and toxins (methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylates) - mnemonic GOLD MARK / MUDPILES.
Gastrointestinal HCO3 loss (diarrhoea), renal tubular acidosis, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, and large-volume saline resuscitation.

redFlags: High-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with a raised osmolar gap -> suspect toxic alcohol (methanol/ethylene glycol) poisoning - time-critical antidote
Severe lactic acidosis -> identify and treat the cause of tissue hypoperfusion/hypoxia urgently

references.label: Merck Manual Professional - Metabolic Acidosis

title: Metabolic alkalosis
summary: Metabolic alkalosis is a primary rise in bicarbonate producing alkalaemia. Classifying by urinary chloride (saline-responsive vs saline-resistant) directs management and is the standard diagnostic approach.

sections.heading: Key findings and classification
items: Primary disorder: pH >7.45 with HCO3 >26 mmol/L
Expected respiratory compensation: PaCO2 rises ~0.7 mmHg for every 1 mmol/L rise in HCO3
Saline-responsive (urine chloride <20 mmol/L): vomiting/NG suction, diuretics, volume depletion
Saline-resistant (urine chloride >20 mmol/L): mineralocorticoid excess (hyperaldosteronism, Cushing), severe hypokalaemia, alkali load

redFlags: Severe metabolic alkalosis (pH >7.55) -> risk of arrhythmia, seizures and reduced cerebral/coronary perfusion; identify and treat the cause and replace potassium
Persistent alkalosis with hypokalaemia and hypertension -> investigate for mineralocorticoid excess

references.label: Merck Manual Professional - Metabolic Alkalosis

title: Mixed acid-base disorders
summary: A mixed disorder is the coexistence of two or more primary acid-base disturbances. They are detected when compensation falls outside the expected range or when both components push the pH in the same direction. The delta-ratio helps detect a second metabolic process.

sections.heading: How to detect a mixed disorder
items: Compensation outside the predicted range (e.g. measured CO2 differs from Winter's-formula prediction) indicates a second disorder
A normal pH with grossly abnormal CO2 and HCO3 suggests two opposing primary disorders
Both CO2 and HCO3 deranged in the direction that worsens the same pH abnormality = combined acidosis or combined alkalosis
Delta ratio (rise in anion gap / fall in HCO3): <1 suggests a coexisting normal-gap acidosis; >2 suggests a coexisting metabolic alkalosis or chronic respiratory acidosis

redFlags: A 'normal' pH can hide two severe opposing disorders - always check CO2 and HCO3 independently

references.label: Merck Manual Professional - Acid-Base Regulation and Disorders (Mixed Disorders)

title: Compensation rules and Winter's formula
summary: Compensation formulae predict the expected secondary response to a primary acid-base disorder. A measured value matching the prediction indicates appropriate single-disorder compensation; deviation signals a mixed disorder. Winter's formula is the standard for metabolic acidosis.

sections.heading: Expected-compensation formulae
items: Metabolic acidosis (Winter's formula): expected PaCO2 (mmHg) = (1.5 x HCO3) + 8 +/- 2
Metabolic alkalosis: expected PaCO2 rises ~0.7 mmHg per 1 mmol/L rise in HCO3
Acute respiratory acidosis: HCO3 rises ~1 mmol/L per 10 mmHg rise in PaCO2
Chronic respiratory acidosis: HCO3 rises ~3.5-4 mmol/L per 10 mmHg rise in PaCO2
Acute respiratory alkalosis: HCO3 falls ~2 mmol/L per 10 mmHg fall in PaCO2
Chronic respiratory alkalosis: HCO3 falls ~4-5 mmol/L per 10 mmHg fall in PaCO2

redFlags: If measured CO2 is higher than Winter's prediction -> coexisting respiratory acidosis (inadequate compensation); if lower -> coexisting respiratory alkalosis

references.label: Winters' Formula for Metabolic Acidosis Compensation (MDCalc)

title: Oxygenation and the alveolar-arterial (A-a) gradient
summary: The A-a gradient compares calculated alveolar oxygen with measured arterial oxygen and helps classify hypoxaemia. A raised gradient indicates a gas-exchange problem (V/Q mismatch, shunt, diffusion defect), whereas a normal gradient points to hypoventilation or low inspired oxygen.

sections.heading: Calculation and interpretation
items: Alveolar gas equation: PAO2 = (FiO2 x (Patm - PH2O)) - (PaCO2 / 0.8); at sea level on room air PAO2 approximately = 150 - (PaCO2/0.8) in mmHg
A-a gradient = PAO2 - PaO2 (use consistent units; both must be on the same FiO2)
Estimated normal upper limit on room air: roughly (Age/4) + 4 mmHg (rises with age and with higher FiO2)
Raised A-a gradient: V/Q mismatch (e.g. PE, pneumonia), right-to-left shunt, diffusion impairment
Normal A-a gradient with hypoxaemia: alveolar hypoventilation (high CO2) or low inspired oxygen (altitude)

redFlags: Hypoxaemia with a raised A-a gradient that does not correct with oxygen -> consider significant shunt
Acute hypoxaemia with a raised A-a gradient and clear chest -> consider pulmonary embolism

references.label: StatPearls - Physiology, Alveolar to Arterial Oxygen Gradient (NCBI)

title: Lactate interpretation
summary: Lactate is a marker of tissue hypoperfusion and metabolic stress. An elevated and especially a rising lactate is associated with worse outcomes; serial measurement and lactate clearance guide resuscitation, notably in sepsis.

sections.heading: Interpretation
items: Normal arterial lactate is approximately <2 mmol/L
Type A (hypoperfusion/hypoxia): shock, sepsis, ischaemia, severe hypoxaemia, post-cardiac arrest
Type B (no overt hypoperfusion): drugs/toxins (metformin, salbutamol, alcohol), liver failure, thiamine deficiency, malignancy, mitochondrial disease
Trend matters: serial lactate and clearance are more informative than a single value
In sepsis, lactate >2 mmol/L marks organ dysfunction and lactate >=4 mmol/L identifies high-risk patients

redFlags: Lactate >=4 mmol/L in suspected sepsis -> high mortality risk; initiate the sepsis bundle and aggressive resuscitation
Rising lactate despite treatment -> ongoing hypoperfusion; escalate care

references.label: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Guidelines 2021 (Critical Care Medicine)

title: Carboxyhaemoglobin and carbon monoxide poisoning
summary: Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin with high affinity, forming carboxyhaemoglobin (COHb) and impairing oxygen delivery. Standard pulse oximetry reads falsely normal; co-oximetry on a blood gas is required. COHb level confirms exposure but correlates poorly with symptom severity.

sections.heading: Interpretation
items: Baseline COHb: ~1-3% in non-smokers; ~10-15% in smokers
Exposure confirmed: >3% in non-smokers, >10% in smokers
Symptomatic poisoning often in the 10-30% range; levels >20% (adults) suggest significant poisoning
Pulse oximetry (SpO2) is falsely reassuring - it cannot distinguish COHb from oxyhaemoglobin; use co-oximetry
COHb level correlates poorly with clinical severity - treat the patient, give high-flow oxygen

redFlags: Suspected CO poisoning -> give high-flow 100% oxygen immediately regardless of SpO2 reading
Loss of consciousness, neurological signs, cardiac ischaemia, pregnancy or high COHb -> discuss hyperbaric oxygen with toxicology

references.label: ATS - Practice Recommendations in the Diagnosis, Management, and Prevention of Carbon Monoxide Poisoning (AJRCCM)

title: Hyponatraemia - diagnostic workup
summary: Hyponatraemia (serum sodium <135 mmol/L) is the commonest electrolyte disturbance. Assessment hinges on serum/plasma osmolality, then volume status, then urine sodium and osmolality. Severity and speed of onset drive the urgency; correction must be controlled to avoid osmotic demyelination.

steps.detail: Measure serum osmolality. Hypotonic (<275 mOsm/kg) hyponatraemia is true; exclude pseudohyponatraemia (high lipids/protein) and hypertonic causes (hyperglycaemia, mannitol).
Hypovolaemic, euvolaemic or hypervolaemic on clinical examination.

Hypovolaemic with urine Na <30 -> extra-renal loss; urine Na >30 -> renal/diuretic loss. Euvolaemic with high urine osmolality and urine Na >30 -> SIADH (diagnosis of exclusion; check thyroid and cortisol).
Heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, renal failure (low urine Na in the first three).

redFlags: Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizures, reduced consciousness, vomiting) -> emergency hypertonic (3%) saline under senior guidance
Correct sodium no faster than ~10 mmol/L in 24 h (less if chronic/high-risk) to avoid osmotic demyelination syndrome

references.label: European clinical practice guideline on diagnosis and treatment of hyponatraemia (Eur J Endocrinol 2014)

title: Hyperkalaemia - causes and next steps
summary: Hyperkalaemia (serum potassium >5.5 mmol/L) is potentially life-threatening through cardiac arrhythmia. First exclude a spurious (haemolysed) sample, then assess severity, obtain an ECG, and identify the cause to guide treatment.

sections.heading: Approach and causes
items: Exclude pseudohyperkalaemia (haemolysis, delayed processing, marked thrombocytosis/leucocytosis) - repeat if clinically unexpected
Severity bands (one common scheme): mild 5.5-5.9, moderate 6.0-6.4, severe >=6.5 mmol/L
Reduced excretion: acute kidney injury / chronic kidney disease, drugs (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, potassium-sparing diuretics, NSAIDs, trimethoprim), hypoaldosteronism / Addison's
Transcellular shift: metabolic acidosis, insulin deficiency/DKA, tissue breakdown (rhabdomyolysis, tumour lysis, haemolysis), digoxin toxicity
Obtain a 12-lead ECG urgently in any significant hyperkalaemia

redFlags: ECG changes of hyperkalaemia, or K+ >=6.5 mmol/L -> emergency treatment: IV calcium for cardioprotection, then insulin-glucose +/- salbutamol to shift, and measures to remove potassium

references.label: Resuscitation Council UK - Emergency treatment of hyperkalaemia (2023)

title: Raised creatinine / acute kidney injury - KDIGO staging
summary: Acute kidney injury is staged by the KDIGO criteria using the rise in serum creatinine and/or fall in urine output, taking the highest stage met by either criterion. Staging guides monitoring, drug review and nephrology referral, and the cause is classified as pre-renal, intrinsic renal or post-renal.

steps.detail: Creatinine 1.5-1.9x baseline OR rise >=26.5 micromol/L (>=0.3 mg/dL) within 48 h; OR urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6-12 h.
Creatinine 2.0-2.9x baseline; OR urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for >=12 h.
Creatinine >=3.0x baseline OR creatinine >=353.6 micromol/L (>=4.0 mg/dL) OR initiation of renal replacement therapy; OR urine output <0.3 mL/kg/h for >=24 h OR anuria >=12 h.

sections.heading: Classify the cause
items: Pre-renal: hypovolaemia, hypotension, sepsis, hepatorenal, cardiorenal
Intrinsic renal: acute tubular necrosis, glomerulonephritis, interstitial nephritis, vasculitis, nephrotoxins
Post-renal: obstruction (stones, prostate, malignancy) - exclude with bladder scan/ultrasound
Review and stop nephrotoxic drugs; check for hyperkalaemia and acidosis

redFlags: AKI with hyperkalaemia, fluid overload/pulmonary oedema, severe acidosis or uraemic complications -> urgent nephrology referral; may need renal replacement therapy
AKI with anuria -> urgently exclude obstruction

references.label: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for Acute Kidney Injury (2012)

title: Abnormal liver function tests - hepatocellular vs cholestatic
summary: An abnormal liver panel is first characterised as predominantly hepatocellular (transaminase-dominant) or cholestatic (ALP/GGT-dominant), which directs the differential. True liver synthetic function is judged by albumin, bilirubin and clotting (INR), not transaminases.

sections.heading: Pattern recognition
items: Hepatocellular: ALT/AST raised out of proportion to ALP -> viral hepatitis, drug/toxin (e.g. paracetamol), ischaemia, autoimmune, alcohol (AST:ALT often >2:1)
Cholestatic: ALP and GGT raised out of proportion to ALT -> biliary obstruction (stones, stricture, tumour), PBC/PSC, drug-induced cholestasis
Isolated raised ALP: confirm hepatic origin with GGT (a raised GGT supports liver/biliary; if GGT normal, consider bone source)
Isolated raised bilirubin: split into unconjugated (haemolysis, Gilbert's) vs conjugated (hepatobiliary)
Synthetic function: low albumin, prolonged INR and rising bilirubin indicate significant liver dysfunction

redFlags: Jaundice with coagulopathy (raised INR) and/or encephalopathy -> acute liver failure; urgent specialist input
Markedly raised transaminases (thousands) -> consider paracetamol toxicity, ischaemic or viral hepatitis

references.label: BSG/EASL - guidance on the management of abnormal liver blood tests (Gut 2018)

title: Raised troponin - causes beyond type 1 MI
summary: Troponin is a sensitive and specific marker of myocardial injury but not of its mechanism. A rise indicates cardiomyocyte damage and must be interpreted with the clinical context, ECG and the rise/fall pattern. Many non-coronary conditions elevate troponin.

sections.heading: Interpretation and differential
items: A dynamic rise and/or fall on serial high-sensitivity troponin indicates acute injury; a stable elevation suggests chronic injury
Type 1 MI: atherothrombotic coronary event (plaque rupture)
Type 2 MI: supply-demand mismatch (tachyarrhythmia, hypotension, anaemia, severe hypertension, sepsis)
Non-ischaemic cardiac causes: myocarditis, heart failure, takotsubo, arrhythmia, cardiac contusion, ablation
Non-cardiac causes: pulmonary embolism, sepsis, chronic kidney disease, stroke/subarachnoid haemorrhage, extreme exertion

redFlags: Rising troponin with ischaemic symptoms or ECG changes -> manage as acute coronary syndrome until excluded
Always interpret troponin against pre-test probability - do not use a single value in isolation to diagnose or exclude MI

references.label: Fourth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction (2018)

title: Anaemia - classification by MCV
summary: Anaemia is efficiently classified by red cell size (mean corpuscular volume) into microcytic, normocytic and macrocytic, each with a characteristic differential. The reticulocyte count and blood film refine the assessment, distinguishing reduced production from increased loss/destruction.

steps.detail: Iron deficiency (commonest), thalassaemia, anaemia of chronic disease (can be normo- or microcytic), sideroblastic anaemia, lead poisoning. Check ferritin/iron studies.
Acute blood loss, anaemia of chronic disease, renal anaemia, mixed deficiency, early iron deficiency, haemolysis, marrow disorders. Use reticulocyte count to separate production vs loss/destruction.
Megaloblastic (B12 or folate deficiency) vs non-megaloblastic (alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, myelodysplasia, certain drugs, reticulocytosis).

redFlags: Severe symptomatic anaemia (chest pain, breathlessness, haemodynamic compromise) -> urgent assessment and consider transfusion
New unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia in an adult -> investigate for gastrointestinal blood loss/malignancy

references.label: Merck Manual Professional - Evaluation of Anemia

title: Thrombocytopenia - approach to a low platelet count
summary: A low platelet count is approached by first excluding spurious (clumping) results on a blood film, then classifying by mechanism: reduced production, increased destruction/consumption, or sequestration. Bleeding risk rises sharply at very low counts, and some causes are medical emergencies.

sections.heading: Approach
items: Exclude pseudothrombocytopenia (EDTA-induced platelet clumping) with a blood film and a citrate sample
Reduced production: marrow infiltration/failure, chemotherapy, B12/folate deficiency, alcohol, viral
Increased destruction/consumption: immune thrombocytopenia (ITP), DIC, thrombotic microangiopathy (TTP/HUS), heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT), sepsis
Sequestration: hypersplenism (e.g. portal hypertension)
Review the blood film for schistocytes (microangiopathy), blasts, or other clues

redFlags: Thrombocytopenia with schistocytes, anaemia and renal/neurological features -> consider TTP/HUS, a haematological emergency
Falling platelets ~5-10 days after heparin with thrombosis -> consider HIT; stop heparin and seek haematology advice
Active bleeding with a very low platelet count -> urgent haematology input and supportive transfusion

references.label: Merck Manual Professional - Thrombocytopenia: Overview

title: Raised white cell count / neutrophilia
summary: A raised white cell count is interpreted by which cell line is elevated. Neutrophilia is most often reactive (infection, inflammation, stress, steroids) but a markedly raised or persistently abnormal count, or abnormal cells on film, raises concern for a haematological process.

sections.heading: Interpretation
items: Identify the predominant cell line on the differential (neutrophils, lymphocytes, eosinophils, monocytes)
Neutrophilia: bacterial infection, tissue inflammation/necrosis, trauma/surgery, corticosteroids, smoking, stress, myeloproliferative disorders
Lymphocytosis: viral infection, pertussis, chronic lymphocytic leukaemia
Eosinophilia: allergy/atopy, parasitic infection, drug reaction, vasculitis
Very high counts, blasts, or persistent unexplained leucocytosis -> blood film and haematology review

redFlags: Leucocytosis with sepsis features -> treat sepsis per pathway; the count itself does not confirm or exclude infection
Neutropenia (low neutrophils) with fever -> neutropenic sepsis, a medical emergency requiring immediate broad-spectrum antibiotics
Blasts on the film or extreme leucocytosis -> urgent haematology referral (possible acute leukaemia)

references.label: Merck Manual Professional - Approach to the Patient With Increased White Blood Cells (Leukocytosis)

title: Raised C-reactive protein (CRP)
summary: CRP is an acute-phase reactant that rises with inflammation, infection and tissue injury. It is sensitive but non-specific and lags behind clinical onset; it cannot by itself diagnose infection or distinguish bacterial from non-bacterial causes. Interpret trends alongside the clinical picture.

sections.heading: Interpretation
items: CRP rises within 6-12 h of an inflammatory stimulus and peaks at ~48 h; a single value can therefore be falsely low early
Common causes of marked elevation: bacterial infection, abscess, tissue necrosis, major trauma/surgery, active inflammatory/autoimmune disease, malignancy
A high CRP does not confirm bacterial infection, and a normal CRP does not exclude serious illness - use with the clinical assessment
Trend (serial CRP) is often more useful than an isolated value for monitoring response to treatment

redFlags: Do not rely on CRP to rule out serious infection in an unwell patient, especially early in the illness - treat on clinical grounds

references.label: NICE NG51 - Sepsis: recognition, diagnosis and early management

title: Abnormal thyroid function tests
summary: Thyroid function is interpreted from the pattern of TSH and free T4 (and T3). TSH is the most sensitive first-line test in stable outpatients; the combination of TSH and free T4 distinguishes primary from secondary disorders and overt from subclinical disease. Avoid testing during acute illness if possible (sick euthyroid).

sections.heading: Pattern interpretation
items: High TSH + low free T4 -> primary hypothyroidism
High TSH + normal free T4 -> subclinical hypothyroidism
Low TSH + high free T4 (and/or T3) -> primary hyperthyroidism
Low TSH + normal free T4 and T3 -> subclinical hyperthyroidism
Low/normal TSH + low free T4 -> secondary (central) hypothyroidism or sick euthyroid; correlate clinically
Non-thyroidal illness (sick euthyroid): variable TSH with low T3/T4 during acute illness - avoid interpreting TFTs in acute illness where possible

redFlags: Severe hyperthyroidism with fever, tachyarrhythmia and altered mental state -> consider thyroid storm, an emergency
Profound hypothyroidism with hypothermia and reduced consciousness -> consider myxoedema coma, an emergency

references.label: NICE NG145 - Thyroid disease: assessment and management

title: Raised calcium (hypercalcaemia)
summary: Always interpret an albumin-corrected calcium. Around 90% of hypercalcaemia is due to primary hyperparathyroidism (often in well outpatients) or malignancy (often in unwell, hospitalised patients). PTH measurement is the pivotal next test.

sections.heading: Approach
items: Use corrected calcium: corrected Ca (mmol/L) = measured Ca + 0.02 x (40 - albumin in g/L)
Check PTH: raised/inappropriately normal PTH -> primary hyperparathyroidism (or familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia); suppressed PTH -> non-PTH cause
Non-PTH causes: malignancy (bony metastases, PTHrP, myeloma), vitamin D excess, granulomatous disease (sarcoidosis, TB), thiazides, milk-alkali
Symptoms ('bones, stones, abdominal groans, psychic moans'): polyuria/polydipsia, constipation, confusion, renal stones

redFlags: Severe hypercalcaemia (corrected Ca >3.0-3.5 mmol/L) or symptomatic -> emergency IV fluid resuscitation and urgent treatment
Hypercalcaemia with dehydration, confusion or arrhythmia -> medical emergency

references.label: Endotext - Hypercalcemia (NCBI Bookshelf)

title: Low calcium (hypocalcaemia)
summary: Confirm hypocalcaemia with an albumin-corrected calcium (or ionised calcium). The differential is organised by PTH (low in hypoparathyroidism; high in vitamin D deficiency and chronic kidney disease). Symptoms relate to neuromuscular irritability.

sections.heading: Approach and signs
items: Use corrected calcium or measure ionised calcium; check magnesium (hypomagnesaemia causes refractory hypocalcaemia)
Low PTH: hypoparathyroidism (post-surgical, autoimmune), hypomagnesaemia
High PTH (secondary): vitamin D deficiency, chronic kidney disease, pseudohypoparathyroidism
Other: acute pancreatitis, tumour lysis, rhabdomyolysis, large citrate load (massive transfusion)
Clinical signs of neuromuscular irritability: perioral/peripheral paraesthesia, Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs, tetany

redFlags: Severe or symptomatic hypocalcaemia (tetany, seizures, laryngospasm, prolonged QT/arrhythmia) -> emergency IV calcium
Always check and correct magnesium - hypocalcaemia will not correct while magnesium is low

references.label: Merck Manual Professional - Hypocalcemia

title: Raised INR / prolonged prothrombin time
summary: A raised INR reflects impaired extrinsic/common pathway clotting. In a patient on a vitamin K antagonist it usually reflects over-anticoagulation; otherwise consider liver disease, vitamin K deficiency, DIC or other coagulopathy. Management depends on the cause and on whether the patient is bleeding.

sections.heading: Causes and approach
items: On warfarin: over-anticoagulation - manage according to INR and bleeding (hold dose, vitamin K, or prothrombin complex concentrate if major bleeding)
Liver disease: reduced synthesis of clotting factors (marker of synthetic function)
Vitamin K deficiency: malnutrition, malabsorption, biliary obstruction, broad-spectrum antibiotics
Disseminated intravascular coagulation: prolonged INR with low fibrinogen, low platelets and raised D-dimer
Note: direct oral anticoagulants can derange INR variably and it should not be used to monitor them

redFlags: Raised INR with major/active bleeding on a vitamin K antagonist -> emergency reversal with prothrombin complex concentrate and IV vitamin K
Prolonged INR with low fibrinogen, low platelets and a precipitating illness -> consider DIC

references.label: British Society for Haematology - Guidelines on oral anticoagulation with warfarin (Br J Haematol)

title: Raised amylase / lipase
summary: Markedly raised pancreatic enzymes support a diagnosis of acute pancreatitis, but lesser elevations are non-specific. Lipase is more sensitive and specific than amylase. The diagnosis of acute pancreatitis requires at least two of three criteria; enzyme level does not predict severity.

sections.heading: Interpretation
items: Diagnosis of acute pancreatitis needs >=2 of: characteristic epigastric pain; amylase or lipase >=3x upper limit of normal; characteristic imaging
Lipase is more sensitive and specific and stays elevated longer than amylase
Enzyme magnitude does NOT correlate with severity - use a severity score and clinical course
Other causes of raised amylase: salivary disease, bowel ischaemia/perforation, ectopic pregnancy, renal impairment, macroamylasaemia, diabetic ketoacidosis

redFlags: Acute pancreatitis with signs of organ dysfunction (hypoxia, hypotension, oliguria) -> severe/critical pancreatitis; escalate care
Severe abdominal pain with raised amylase but atypical features -> consider bowel ischaemia or perforation

references.label: Merck Manual Professional - Acute Pancreatitis

title: Ferritin interpretation
summary: Ferritin reflects body iron stores but is also an acute-phase reactant, so it rises with inflammation, liver disease and malignancy. A low ferritin is highly specific for iron deficiency; a normal or raised ferritin does not exclude it when inflammation is present.

sections.heading: Interpretation
items: Low ferritin -> confirms iron deficiency (highly specific). NICE uses a ferritin <30 microgram/L to diagnose iron deficiency
Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant: inflammation, infection, liver disease and malignancy raise it independent of iron stores
In the presence of inflammation, iron deficiency can coexist with a normal/raised ferritin - check transferrin saturation / CRP to interpret
Very high ferritin: consider iron overload (haemochromatosis, repeated transfusion), severe inflammation, or haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis

redFlags: Markedly elevated ferritin with fever, cytopenias and organ dysfunction -> consider haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH), a life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome

references.label: NICE CKS - Anaemia - iron deficiency (diagnosis)

title: Raised D-dimer
summary: D-dimer is a fibrin degradation product that is sensitive but very non-specific for venous thromboembolism. Its value is in ruling OUT VTE in patients with low/non-high pre-test probability; it should not be used to rule in VTE or ordered without a pre-test probability assessment.

sections.heading: Interpretation
items: Use only after a validated pre-test probability score (e.g. Wells): a negative D-dimer in a low/unlikely-probability patient safely excludes VTE
A raised D-dimer is non-specific and does NOT confirm VTE - proceed to imaging when probability is raised
Consider age-adjusted D-dimer cut-offs in patients over 50 to improve specificity
Other causes of a raised D-dimer: infection/sepsis, malignancy, pregnancy, recent surgery/trauma, inflammation, advanced age, DIC
Do not send a D-dimer in a high pre-test probability patient - go straight to imaging

redFlags: Do not use D-dimer to exclude VTE in high pre-test probability patients - arrange definitive imaging

references.label: NICE NG158 - Venous thromboembolic diseases: diagnosis, management and thrombophilia testing

title: Suspected pulmonary embolism - imaging selection
summary: Imaging for suspected PE is driven by a validated pre-test probability (Wells score) combined with D-dimer. The two-level Wells score determines whether to image directly or to use D-dimer first; CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) is the usual first-line test, with V/Q (or V/Q SPECT) reserved for specific situations.

sections.heading: Two-level Wells score for PE (points)
items: Clinical signs/symptoms of DVT: 3
PE is the most likely diagnosis (alternative less likely): 3
Heart rate >100/min: 1.5
Immobilisation >=3 days or surgery in the previous 4 weeks: 1.5
Previous DVT/PE: 1.5
Haemoptysis: 1
Active cancer (treatment within 6 months or palliative): 1

sections.heading: Decision pathway
items: PE likely (score >4): arrange immediate CTPA; if delay, give interim anticoagulation. If CTPA negative, consider proximal leg vein ultrasound if DVT suspected
PE unlikely (score <=4): perform a D-dimer; if positive, arrange CTPA; if negative, PE excluded and consider an alternative diagnosis
Use V/Q (or V/Q SPECT) scan as an alternative to CTPA in renal impairment, contrast allergy, or pregnancy considerations
In pregnancy, follow specific pathways (chest X-ray first, then V/Q or CTPA per local protocol)

redFlags: Suspected PE with haemodynamic instability (hypotension) -> high-risk PE; consider immediate bedside echo and emergency reperfusion - do not delay for elective imaging

references.label: NICE NG158 - Venous thromboembolic diseases: diagnosis and management

title: Head injury - when to CT the head
summary: Validated rules (NICE head injury criteria; Canadian CT Head Rule) identify which adults with head injury need CT to detect clinically important brain injury. Selecting on these criteria avoids missing serious injury while limiting unnecessary imaging.

sections.heading: Canadian CT Head Rule (minor head injury, GCS 13-15)
items: High-risk (CT to identify neurosurgical lesion): GCS <15 at 2 hours post-injury; suspected open or depressed skull fracture; any sign of basal skull fracture; >=2 episodes of vomiting; age >=65 years
Medium-risk (CT to detect brain injury on imaging): amnesia before impact >30 minutes; dangerous mechanism (pedestrian struck, ejection from vehicle, fall from >3 feet or 5 stairs)
The rule applies to minor head injury with witnessed loss of consciousness, amnesia or disorientation; it excludes anticoagulated patients, seizures and certain other groups

sections.heading: Additional NICE criteria for CT within 1 hour
items: GCS <13 on initial assessment, or GCS <15 at 2 hours
Suspected open/depressed skull fracture or any sign of basal skull fracture
Post-traumatic seizure
Focal neurological deficit
More than one episode of vomiting
CT within 8 hours for patients on anticoagulants who have sustained a head injury (even without other risk factors)

redFlags: GCS <=8 -> secure the airway and obtain urgent CT; involve anaesthetics/critical care
Anticoagulated head injury -> low threshold for CT even with a normal GCS

references.label: NICE NG232 - Head injury: assessment and early management

title: Suspected acute stroke - imaging selection
summary: Suspected acute stroke needs urgent brain imaging to distinguish ischaemic from haemorrhagic stroke before reperfusion treatment. Non-contrast CT is the immediate first-line study; CT angiography and perfusion imaging guide thrombectomy decisions in eligible patients.

sections.heading: Imaging pathway
items: Perform urgent non-contrast CT head immediately (and within established time targets) to exclude haemorrhage before thrombolysis

Image immediately (within 1 hour) if any of: indication for thrombolysis/thrombectomy, on anticoagulants, known bleeding tendency, depressed consciousness (GCS <13), unexplained progressive/fluctuating symptoms, papilloedema/neck stiffness/fever, or severe headache at onset
CT angiography to identify large-vessel occlusion when mechanical thrombectomy is being considered
CT perfusion or MRI may extend the eligibility window for thrombectomy in selected patients

redFlags: Sudden focal neurological deficit -> treat as stroke; emergency imaging and stroke pathway activation are time-critical (time is brain)
Imaging showing haemorrhage -> stop/avoid antithrombotics and arrange urgent neurosurgical/stroke review

references.label: NICE NG128 - Stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s: diagnosis and initial management

title: Cervical spine - when to image (Canadian C-spine / NEXUS)
summary: Two validated rules identify alert, stable blunt-trauma patients who do not need cervical spine imaging: the Canadian C-Spine Rule and the NEXUS criteria. CT is the preferred imaging modality when imaging is indicated in significant trauma.

steps.detail: Age >=65 years; dangerous mechanism (fall from >=1 m / 5 stairs, axial load to head, high-speed MVC >100 km/h, rollover/ejection, motorised recreational vehicle, bicycle collision); or paraesthesia in the extremities.

steps.step: Low-risk factors -> assess range of motion
steps.detail: If no high-risk factor and at least one low-risk factor present (simple rear-end collision, sitting position in ED, ambulatory at any time, delayed onset of neck pain, absence of midline tenderness), test active rotation.
If the patient can actively rotate the neck 45 degrees left and right, no imaging is needed. If unable, image.

sections.heading: NEXUS criteria (no imaging if ALL five are met)
items: No posterior midline cervical-spine tenderness
No focal neurological deficit
Normal alertness/level of consciousness
No evidence of intoxication
No painful distracting injury

redFlags: Any high-risk feature, focal neurology, or failure of a clearance rule -> immobilise and image (CT preferred in significant trauma)

references.label: Stiell IG et al. The Canadian C-Spine Rule versus the NEXUS Low-Risk Criteria (NEJM 2003)

title: Suspected appendicitis - imaging selection
summary: Imaging in suspected appendicitis is tailored to age, sex and pregnancy. Ultrasound is preferred first-line in children and pregnant women (no ionising radiation); CT has the highest accuracy in adults; MRI is an alternative in pregnancy when ultrasound is inconclusive.

sections.heading: Modality by group
items: Children and young/thin adults: ultrasound first (no radiation); proceed to MRI or CT if inconclusive
Pregnant women: ultrasound first-line; MRI if ultrasound is inconclusive (avoid CT radiation where possible)
Non-pregnant adults: CT of the abdomen and pelvis has the highest diagnostic accuracy
A clinical scoring tool (e.g. Alvarado) can support risk-stratification but does not replace imaging/surgical assessment

redFlags: Peritonitis, haemodynamic instability or features of perforation -> urgent surgical assessment; do not delay for imaging if the patient needs theatre

references.label: ACR Appropriateness Criteria - Right Lower Quadrant Pain / Suspected Appendicitis

title: Suspected renal colic - imaging selection
summary: For suspected renal/ureteric colic, low-dose non-contrast CT of the kidneys, ureters and bladder (CT KUB) is the investigation of choice in adults because of its high sensitivity for stones. Ultrasound is preferred first-line in pregnancy and in children.

sections.heading: Modality selection
items: Adults with suspected ureteric stone: offer low-dose non-contrast CT KUB (first-line, high sensitivity and specificity)
Pregnant women: ultrasound first-line (no ionising radiation)
Children and young people: ultrasound first-line; consider low-dose CT if ultrasound does not detect a stone and there is ongoing clinical suspicion
CT also identifies alternative diagnoses (e.g. abdominal aortic aneurysm) that can mimic renal colic

redFlags: Suspected renal colic with fever/sepsis and an obstructing stone -> urological emergency (infected obstructed system) needing urgent decompression
Older patient with 'renal colic' and cardiovascular risk -> actively exclude a leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm

references.label: NICE NG118 - Renal and ureteric stones: assessment and management

title: Suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage - imaging selection
summary: In suspected aneurysmal SAH (sudden severe 'thunderclap' headache), urgent non-contrast CT head is first-line. CT sensitivity is highest very early; a negative CT performed within 6 hours of a non-traumatic thunderclap headache effectively excludes SAH in many patients, with lumbar puncture used when CT is later or equivocal.

sections.heading: Pathway
items: Immediate non-contrast CT head: sensitivity is very high when performed within 6 hours of symptom onset
If CT is negative and performed within 6 hours in a typical thunderclap presentation, SAH is very unlikely (per modern emergency practice)
If CT is negative and performed after 6 hours, or is equivocal, perform lumbar puncture - timed at least 12 hours after headache onset to detect xanthochromia
CT/MR angiography is used to identify an aneurysm once SAH is confirmed

redFlags: Sudden severe 'worst-ever' (thunderclap) headache -> emergency imaging; SAH is a neurosurgical emergency
Confirmed SAH -> urgent neurosurgical referral and blood pressure/rebleeding management

references.label: Perry JJ et al. Sensitivity of computed tomography for acute subarachnoid haemorrhage (BMJ 2011)

title: Ankle and knee injury - Ottawa rules for X-ray
summary: The Ottawa Ankle and Foot Rules and the Ottawa Knee Rule are highly sensitive decision rules that identify which acute injuries require X-ray, safely reducing imaging in low-risk patients. They are validated in adults (and the ankle rules in children over ~5 years).

sections.heading: Ottawa Ankle and Foot Rules
items: Ankle X-ray indicated if pain in the malleolar zone AND any of: bone tenderness at the posterior edge/tip of the lateral malleolus (distal 6 cm of fibula), bone tenderness at the posterior edge/tip of the medial malleolus (distal 6 cm of tibia), OR inability to bear weight (4 steps) both immediately and in the ED

Foot X-ray indicated if pain in the midfoot zone AND any of: bone tenderness at the base of the 5th metatarsal, bone tenderness at the navicular, OR inability to bear weight (4 steps) both immediately and in the ED

sections.heading: Ottawa Knee Rule (X-ray if any present)
items: Age >=55 years
Isolated tenderness of the patella
Tenderness at the head of the fibula
Inability to flex the knee to 90 degrees
Inability to bear weight (4 steps) both immediately and in the ED

references.label: Stiell IG, Greenberg GH, McKnight RD, Nair RC, McDowell I, Reardon M, Stewart JP, Maloney J. Decision rules for the use of radiography in acute ankle injuries. JAMA 1993;269(9):1127-32.
Stiell IG et al. Derivation of a decision rule for the use of radiography in acute knee injuries. Ann Emerg Med 1995;26(4):405-13.

title: Chest X-ray - common indications
summary: The chest radiograph is a first-line study for many cardiorespiratory presentations and for confirming device/line position. Knowing the appropriate indications (and the limits of plain film) directs efficient imaging, with CT reserved for problems the plain film cannot resolve.

sections.heading: Common appropriate indications
items: Suspected pneumonia / lower respiratory tract infection with focal signs or systemic illness
Acute breathlessness, suspected heart failure (pulmonary oedema), or pleural effusion
Suspected pneumothorax (erect film; consider expiratory views/CT if equivocal)
Chest trauma assessment and suspected rib fractures with respiratory compromise
Confirmation of central line, endotracheal tube, chest drain or nasogastric tube position
Haemoptysis, and as part of the workup of suspected lung malignancy
Note: a normal chest X-ray does not exclude PE or early/atypical infection - escalate to CT when clinically indicated

redFlags: Do not delay decompression of a tension pneumothorax to obtain a chest X-ray - it is a clinical diagnosis requiring immediate treatment
Nasogastric tube feeding must not begin until correct position is confirmed (pH test or X-ray per protocol)

references.label: Royal College of Radiologists - iRefer: Making the best use of clinical radiology

title: Suspected bowel obstruction - abdominal imaging
summary: For suspected bowel obstruction, contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis is the investigation of choice in adults: it confirms obstruction, identifies the level and cause, and detects complications such as ischaemia or perforation. Plain films are less sensitive and largely superseded by CT.

sections.heading: Modality selection
items: Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen/pelvis: first-line in adults - confirms obstruction, defines level (small vs large bowel) and cause, and detects strangulation/ischaemia and perforation
Plain abdominal X-ray: limited sensitivity; may show dilated loops but a normal film does not exclude obstruction - do not rely on it
Erect chest X-ray: useful to detect free air under the diaphragm in suspected perforation
Water-soluble contrast follow-through can have a therapeutic and prognostic role in adhesional small-bowel obstruction
Ultrasound is preferred first in children with suspected intussusception

redFlags: Signs of strangulation/ischaemia (severe constant pain, peritonism, raised lactate) or perforation -> surgical emergency; urgent CT and surgical review
Closed-loop obstruction or volvulus -> high risk of ischaemia, requires urgent surgical management

references.label: ACR Appropriateness Criteria - Suspected Small-Bowel Obstruction

title: Paced rhythms on ECG
summary: Cardiac pacing produces electrical pacing spikes followed by a paced complex. Recognising atrial, ventricular and dual-chamber pacing, and confirming appropriate capture and sensing, is the bedside task. Right ventricular pacing produces an LBBB-like morphology, which obscures standard ischaemia interpretation (use modified Sgarbossa criteria).

sections.heading: Recognition
items: Pacing spike: a narrow, vertical deflection immediately preceding the captured complex
Atrial pacing: spike before a P wave (capture confirmed by a following P wave)
Ventricular pacing: spike before a broad QRS, typically LBBB-like morphology with left axis when paced from the RV apex
Dual-chamber (DDD) pacing: an atrial spike then a ventricular spike (AV sequential)
Appropriate capture: every pacing spike is followed by the expected depolarisation; appropriate sensing: pacing is inhibited by intrinsic beats

sections.heading: Pacemaker malfunction patterns
items: Failure to capture: pacing spike not followed by depolarisation
Failure to sense (undersensing): pacing spikes appear despite intrinsic beats
Oversensing: expected pacing spikes are absent because the device misreads other signals as intrinsic activity
Ventricular-paced rhythm mimics LBBB - use modified Sgarbossa criteria to assess for acute MI

redFlags: Failure to capture in a pacemaker-dependent patient -> bradycardia/asystole risk; urgent cardiology and consider transcutaneous pacing
Wide-complex tachycardia with pacing spikes -> consider pacemaker-mediated tachycardia and apply a magnet / seek device interrogation

references.label: 2021 ESC Guidelines on cardiac pacing and cardiac resynchronization therapy (Eur Heart J)

title: Junctional rhythm on ECG
summary: A junctional rhythm arises from the AV junction when the sinus node fails or is suppressed. The escape rate is typically 40-60/min with a narrow QRS and absent, inverted or retrograde P waves. It is usually an escape mechanism, so the priority is to identify and treat the cause of sinus node failure or AV block.

sections.heading: Key findings
items: Narrow QRS (junctional origin) at a regular rate
P waves absent, or inverted in the inferior leads (II, III, aVF), occurring just before, during or just after the QRS (retrograde atrial activation)
Junctional escape rate ~40-60/min; accelerated junctional rhythm ~60-100/min; junctional tachycardia >100/min
Often seen with increased vagal tone, sick sinus syndrome, inferior MI, digoxin toxicity or after cardiac surgery

redFlags: Junctional rhythm with bradycardia and adverse signs (shock, syncope, heart failure, ischaemia) -> follow bradycardia algorithm
Accelerated junctional rhythm in a patient on digoxin -> consider digoxin toxicity

references.label: Mason JW, Hancock EW, Gettes LS. AHA/ACCF/HRS recommendations for the standardization and interpretation of the ECG: Part II. Electrocardiography diagnostic statement list. Circulation 2007;115(10):1325-1332.

title: Multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT)
summary: MAT is an irregular supraventricular tachycardia arising from multiple atrial ectopic foci, defined by at least three distinct non-sinus P-wave morphologies in a single lead with an atrial rate >100/min. It is strongly associated with COPD and other pulmonary disease, and management is primarily of the underlying condition.

sections.heading: Diagnostic criteria
items: Atrial rate >100/min
At least three distinct non-sinus P-wave morphologies in a single lead
Irregular PP, PR and RR intervals with an isoelectric baseline between P waves
Distinguish from atrial fibrillation: MAT has discrete, identifiable (if varying) P waves, whereas AF has no organised P waves

redFlags: MAT usually reflects severe underlying illness (decompensated COPD, sepsis, hypoxia, electrolyte disturbance) - treat the cause
AV-nodal blocking drugs are often ineffective and beta-blockers may be contraindicated in bronchospasm

references.label: StatPearls - Multifocal Atrial Tachycardia (NCBI)

title: Distinguishing AVNRT from AVRT
summary: AVNRT and orthodromic AVRT are the two commonest paroxysmal regular narrow-complex SVTs. Both present as a regular tachycardia ~150-250/min, but the position of the retrograde P wave relative to the QRS helps distinguish them. Definitive distinction is electrophysiological; the acute treatment (vagal manoeuvres, adenosine) is the same.

sections.heading: Distinguishing features
items: AVNRT (re-entry within the AV node): P wave usually buried in or very close to the QRS; may produce a pseudo-R' in V1 or pseudo-S in inferior leads (very short RP)
Orthodromic AVRT (re-entry via an accessory pathway): retrograde P wave clearly separated after the QRS (longer RP), often inverted in inferior leads
AVRT implies an accessory pathway - look for a delta wave / WPW pattern on a resting ECG once in sinus rhythm
Both terminate with vagal manoeuvres or adenosine, which is also diagnostic

redFlags: Any SVT with haemodynamic instability -> synchronised cardioversion
If a resting ECG shows pre-excitation (WPW), avoid AV-nodal blockers if the patient ever develops irregular pre-excited AF

references.label: 2019 ESC Guidelines for supraventricular tachycardia (Eur Heart J)

title: Wellens syndrome
summary: Wellens syndrome is a pattern of deeply inverted or biphasic T waves in V2-V3 that is highly specific for critical proximal LAD stenosis. Patients are often pain-free at the time of the ECG with normal or minimally raised troponin, but are at high risk of an impending large anterior MI. Stress testing is dangerous; angiography is indicated.

sections.heading: Key findings
items: Type A (~25%): biphasic T waves in V2-V3
Type B (~75%): deeply and symmetrically inverted T waves in V2-V3 (may extend to V1-V6)
Recorded typically when the patient is pain-free (a pain-free interval after recent anginal chest pain)
Little or no ST elevation; no pathological precordial Q waves; preserved R-wave progression; normal or minimally elevated troponin

redFlags: Wellens pattern -> critical proximal LAD stenosis; refer for urgent invasive coronary angiography
Avoid stress testing - it can precipitate an extensive anterior infarction

references.label: StatPearls - Wellens Syndrome (NCBI)

title: Brugada syndrome / pattern
summary: Brugada syndrome is an inherited sodium-channelopathy associated with sudden cardiac death from polymorphic VT/VF. Only the type 1 (coved) pattern is diagnostic. The pattern is dynamic and can be unmasked by fever, sodium-channel-blocking drugs and other provocations, so a normal ECG does not exclude it.

sections.heading: ECG patterns
items: Type 1 (diagnostic): coved ST-segment elevation >=2 mm in >=1 right precordial lead (V1-V2), with the ST segment descending into an inverted T wave
Type 2: 'saddleback' ST elevation with >=0.5 mm elevation (not diagnostic alone)
The pattern is dynamic; it may be intermittent or concealed
Provoking factors: fever, sodium-channel blockers (e.g. flecainide), tricyclics, cocaine, electrolyte disturbance

redFlags: Type 1 Brugada pattern, especially with syncope or a family history of sudden death -> urgent cardiology/electrophysiology referral for risk stratification
Treat fever promptly with antipyretics, as fever can unmask the pattern and precipitate arrhythmia

references.label: StatPearls - Brugada Syndrome (NCBI)

title: Osborn (J) waves and hypothermia
summary: The Osborn (J) wave is a positive deflection at the J point (the QRS-ST junction), classically seen in hypothermia, where its amplitude broadly increases as temperature falls. Hypothermia also causes bradycardia, interval prolongation and a high risk of ventricular arrhythmia with rough handling.

sections.heading: Key findings
items: Osborn (J) wave: a notch or hump at the J point, best seen in the inferior and lateral leads; amplitude tends to increase with deeper hypothermia
Bradycardia (sinus bradycardia, slow AF)
Prolongation of PR, QRS and QT intervals
Shivering or muscle-tremor artefact on the baseline
Osborn waves are not specific to hypothermia (also seen in hypercalcaemia, severe CNS injury, early repolarisation)

redFlags: Severe hypothermia -> myocardium is irritable; minimise rough handling and unnecessary movement to avoid precipitating VF
Bradyarrhythmia in hypothermia may be refractory until the patient is rewarmed

references.label: Lott C et al. European Resuscitation Council Guidelines 2021: Cardiac arrest in special circumstances. Resuscitation 2021;161:152-219.
Vanden Hoek TL et al. Part 12: Cardiac Arrest in Special Situations: 2010 American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and ECC. Circulation 2010;122(18 Suppl 3):S829-S861.

title: Electrical alternans and cardiac tamponade
summary: Electrical alternans is a beat-to-beat alternation in QRS amplitude caused by the heart swinging within a large pericardial effusion. In the right context it strongly suggests pericardial effusion with possible tamponade, which is a clinical and echocardiographic diagnosis requiring urgent assessment.

sections.heading: Key findings
items: Beat-to-beat alternation in QRS amplitude (and sometimes P/T waves) at a constant rate
Often accompanied by low QRS voltage and sinus tachycardia in a large effusion
The triad of electrical alternans, low voltage and tachycardia is suggestive of a large pericardial effusion
Tamponade is a clinical/echocardiographic diagnosis (hypotension, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds, pulsus paradoxus); the ECG is only supportive

redFlags: Electrical alternans with haemodynamic compromise -> suspect cardiac tamponade; urgent echocardiography and consider pericardiocentesis
Pulseless electrical activity with a known large effusion -> consider tamponade as a reversible cause of arrest

references.label: 2015 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of pericardial diseases (Eur Heart J)

title: Torsades de pointes
summary: Torsades de pointes is a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia occurring on a background of QT prolongation, characterised by QRS complexes that appear to twist around the baseline. It can self-terminate or degenerate into VF. IV magnesium and correction of precipitants are the priorities.

sections.heading: Key findings
items: Polymorphic VT with a continuously changing QRS axis - complexes appear to twist around the isoelectric baseline
Occurs in the context of a prolonged QT interval (drug-induced, electrolyte disturbance, congenital long QT)
Often initiated by a premature ventricular beat falling on the T wave (R-on-T), frequently after a pause (pause-dependent)
Rate typically 200-250/min; episodes may be self-limiting or sustained

redFlags: Torsades de pointes -> give IV magnesium sulphate; stop QT-prolonging drugs and correct potassium/magnesium
Sustained torsades with a pulse and instability, or degeneration to VF -> defibrillate / cardiovert per ALS
Recurrent pause-dependent torsades -> consider overdrive pacing or isoprenaline to raise the heart rate

references.label: 2022 ESC Guidelines for ventricular arrhythmias and prevention of sudden cardiac death (Eur Heart J)

title: Sgarbossa criteria - diagnosing MI in LBBB or paced rhythm
summary: Because LBBB (and ventricular pacing) produce secondary ST/T changes, standard STEMI criteria cannot be applied. The Sgarbossa criteria, and the Smith-modified version, identify acute MI in this setting. The modified third criterion uses a proportional (ST/S ratio) cut-off and is markedly more sensitive.

sections.heading: Criteria
items: Concordant ST elevation >=1 mm in a lead with a positive (upward) QRS - highly specific (original score 5)
Concordant ST depression >=1 mm in V1, V2 or V3 (original score 3)
Original third criterion: discordant ST elevation >=5 mm in a lead with a negative QRS (less specific; original score 2)
Modified (Smith) third criterion: discordant ST elevation that is proportionally excessive, ST elevation >=25% of the depth of the preceding S wave (ST/S ratio <= -0.25)
Original criteria specific (~98%) but insensitive (~20%); the modified criteria improve sensitivity to ~80% while keeping specificity ~99%

redFlags: Any positive Sgarbossa/Smith-modified criterion in a patient with ischaemic symptoms and LBBB or ventricular pacing -> treat as acute coronary occlusion and activate the reperfusion pathway
A negative score does not exclude MI - use serial ECGs, troponin and the clinical picture

references.label: Sgarbossa EB et al. Electrocardiographic diagnosis of evolving acute MI in the presence of LBBB (NEJM 1996)
Meyers HP, Smith SW et al. Validation of the modified Sgarbossa criteria (original Smith derivation 2012)

title: Delta ratio (delta-delta gap)
