summary: In a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, the delta ratio compares the rise in the anion gap with the fall in bicarbonate to detect a coexisting second metabolic disorder. It assumes that, in a pure high-anion-gap acidosis, each added acid consumes roughly one bicarbonate.

sections.heading: Calculation and interpretation
items: Delta ratio = (measured anion gap - normal anion gap) / (normal HCO3 - measured HCO3), using a normal anion gap of ~12 and normal HCO3 of ~24 mmol/L
Ratio <0.4: pure normal-anion-gap (hyperchloraemic) metabolic acidosis
Ratio 0.4-1: a coexisting normal-anion-gap acidosis alongside the high-anion-gap acidosis
Ratio 1-2: pure high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis (the expected range)
Ratio >2: a coexisting metabolic alkalosis or a pre-existing high HCO3 (e.g. chronic respiratory acidosis)

redFlags: Use the delta ratio only after confirming a raised anion gap; it is an adjunct, interpreted with the clinical picture and the other compensation rules

references.label: Berend K, de Vries APJ, Gans ROB. Physiological approach to assessment of acid-base disturbances. N Engl J Med 2014;371(15):1434-1445.

title: Osmolar (osmolal) gap
summary: The osmolar gap is the difference between the measured serum osmolality and the calculated osmolarity. A raised gap indicates unmeasured osmotically active solutes, classically the toxic alcohols (methanol, ethylene glycol). It is most useful early, before the alcohol is metabolised to its acid (which then raises the anion gap).

sections.heading: Calculation and interpretation
items: Calculated osmolarity (mmol/L) = 2 x Na + glucose + urea (all in mmol/L); add ethanol (mmol/L) if measured
Osmolar gap = measured osmolality - calculated osmolarity
Normal osmolar gap is approximately <10-15 mOsm/kg (a normal gap does not exclude toxic alcohol ingestion)
Causes of a raised gap: methanol, ethylene glycol, ethanol, isopropanol, propylene glycol, mannitol, severe ketoacidosis/lactic acidosis
Sequence in toxic alcohols: early high osmolar gap with normal anion gap; later, as the parent alcohol is metabolised, the osmolar gap falls and a high anion gap (acid) appears

redFlags: Raised osmolar gap with a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis -> strongly suspect methanol or ethylene glycol poisoning; this is time-critical (fomepizole/ethanol, dialysis)
A normal osmolar gap does not exclude toxic alcohol poisoning, especially late after ingestion

references.label: UI Health Care - Osmolality Gap: Calculation and Interpretation

title: Salicylate poisoning - mixed acid-base picture
summary: Salicylate (aspirin) toxicity produces a characteristic mixed acid-base disturbance: an early primary respiratory alkalosis from direct stimulation of the respiratory centre, combined with a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. Recognising this pattern in a patient with hyperventilation, tinnitus and confusion should prompt a salicylate level.

sections.heading: Key findings
items: Classic mixed picture: primary respiratory alkalosis AND high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis occurring together
Early: respiratory alkalosis predominates (low PaCO2, raised pH) from direct medullary stimulation
Later: high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis develops (raised lactate, ketones, salicylate) and may dominate, especially in children and severe poisoning
A near-normal or falling pH in salicylate poisoning is a worrying sign of decompensation
Associated clinical clues: tinnitus, hyperventilation, sweating, vomiting, agitation, hyperthermia

redFlags: A falling pH (acidaemia) in salicylate poisoning is dangerous - acidaemia increases CNS salicylate penetration; avoid hypoventilation where possible and seek toxicology advice
Severe poisoning, CNS features, acidaemia or very high levels -> urgent discussion regarding urinary alkalinisation and haemodialysis

references.label: Merck Manual Professional - Aspirin and Other Salicylate Poisoning

title: Methaemoglobinaemia on co-oximetry
summary: Methaemoglobin contains iron in the ferric (Fe3+) state, which cannot carry oxygen and shifts the dissociation curve, impairing delivery. Standard pulse oximetry is unreliable and tends to read toward ~85%; the diagnosis is made by co-oximetry on a blood gas. Cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen with a normal PaO2 is the classic clue.

sections.heading: Key findings
items: Co-oximetry reports an elevated methaemoglobin fraction (normal <1-2%)
PaO2 (dissolved oxygen) is normal despite clinical cyanosis - oxygen content is reduced because functional haemoglobin is low
Pulse oximetry is unreliable and classically tends toward ~85% regardless of true saturation
'Chocolate-brown' arterial blood that does not redden on exposure to air is a classic sign
Common precipitants: dapsone, local anaesthetics (benzocaine, prilocaine), nitrites/nitrates, some antimalarials

redFlags: Symptomatic methaemoglobinaemia (typically levels >20-30%, or lower if comorbid) -> consider IV methylene blue and stop the offending agent
Avoid methylene blue in known G6PD deficiency (ineffective and may cause haemolysis) - seek toxicology advice

references.label: StatPearls - Methemoglobinemia (NCBI)

title: Base excess and standard base excess
summary: Base excess (BE) quantifies the metabolic component of an acid-base disturbance: the amount of acid or base needed to return blood pH to 7.40 at a PaCO2 of 40 mmHg. It is independent of the respiratory component and is a useful quick marker of metabolic acidosis or alkalosis severity.

sections.heading: Interpretation
items: Normal base excess: approximately -2 to +2 mmol/L
Negative base excess (base deficit) more negative than -2: a metabolic acidosis
Positive base excess greater than +2: a metabolic alkalosis
Standard base excess (SBE) is calculated for the whole extracellular fluid and is more stable across changing PaCO2
A large base deficit in trauma/shock correlates with the degree of hypoperfusion and is a useful resuscitation marker (interpret alongside lactate)

redFlags: A large and worsening base deficit in a shocked patient -> ongoing tissue hypoperfusion; escalate resuscitation and seek the cause

references.label: Berend K, de Vries APJ, Gans ROB. Physiological approach to assessment of acid-base disturbances. N Engl J Med 2014;371(15):1434-1445.

title: Venous vs arterial blood gas - agreement and limits
summary: A venous blood gas (VBG) is a reasonable substitute for an arterial gas for pH and bicarbonate in many settings, sparing an arterial puncture. However, the agreement breaks down for oxygenation and at the extremes of carbon dioxide, so a VBG must be interpreted with these limits in mind.

sections.heading: What agrees and what does not
items: pH: venous pH runs slightly lower than arterial, by roughly 0.03-0.04 units; generally good agreement and adequate for trend
Bicarbonate: venous HCO3 agrees closely with arterial (typically within ~1-2 mmol/L)

PvCO2: runs a few mmHg higher than arterial; a normal venous CO2 makes significant arterial hypercapnia unlikely, but agreement is poor when CO2 is high (do not rely on a VBG to titrate CO2 in hypercapnic respiratory failure)
Oxygenation: venous PO2 and saturation do NOT reflect arterial oxygenation - use an arterial sample or SpO2 to assess oxygenation
A VBG is useful for pH, HCO3, lactate, electrolytes and to screen out hypercapnia; an ABG is needed when accurate PaO2 or PaCO2 is essential

redFlags: Never assess oxygenation from a venous gas
Do not rely on a VBG to exclude or quantify hypercapnia in a patient with respiratory failure - confirm with an arterial sample

references.label: Byrne AL et al. Peripheral venous and arterial blood gas analysis in adults: a systematic review (Respirology 2014)

title: Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC) on ECG
summary: ARVC is an inherited cardiomyopathy with fibrofatty replacement of the right ventricle, predisposing to ventricular arrhythmias and sudden death, particularly in young people and athletes. ECG features are part of the Task Force diagnostic criteria; the epsilon wave and right precordial T-wave inversion are characteristic.

sections.heading: Key findings
items: Epsilon wave: a small reproducible deflection at the end of the QRS in the right precordial leads (V1-V3) - a major criterion
T-wave inversion in the right precordial leads (V1-V3) beyond age 14, without RBBB
Localised QRS prolongation / terminal activation delay in V1-V3
Ventricular ectopy and VT with a left bundle branch block morphology (RV origin), classically superior axis

redFlags: Young patient or athlete with syncope, exertional palpitations or VT of LBBB morphology -> consider ARVC; urgent cardiology referral
Family history of sudden cardiac death plus right precordial ECG changes -> investigate for inherited cardiomyopathy

references.label: Marcus FI et al. Revised Task Force Criteria for ARVC (Circulation 2010)

title: Low QRS voltage on ECG
summary: Low QRS voltage describes abnormally small QRS amplitudes and may reflect either reduced cardiac signal (infiltration, effusion) or attenuation between heart and electrodes (obesity, emphysema, oedema). It is a clue, not a diagnosis, and is interpreted with the clinical context.

sections.heading: Definition and causes
items: Limb-lead low voltage: QRS amplitude <5 mm in all limb leads
Precordial low voltage: QRS amplitude <10 mm in all precordial leads
Attenuation (extracardiac): obesity, pericardial effusion, large pleural effusion, emphysema/COPD, subcutaneous oedema (anasarca)
Reduced myocardial signal: infiltrative disease (amyloidosis), extensive infarction, myxoedema, end-stage cardiomyopathy
Low voltage with sinus tachycardia and electrical alternans suggests a large pericardial effusion

redFlags: New low voltage with sinus tachycardia, raised JVP and hypotension -> consider pericardial effusion / tamponade and obtain urgent echocardiography

references.label: Hancock EW, Deal BJ, Mirvis DM, Okin P, Kligfield P, Gettes LS. AHA/ACCF/HRS recommendations for the standardization and interpretation of the ECG: Part V. Electrocardiogram changes associated with cardiac chamber hypertrophy. Circulation 2009;119(10):e251-e261.

title: P-mitrale and P-pulmonale (atrial enlargement) on ECG
summary: Abnormal P-wave morphology reflects atrial enlargement. P-mitrale indicates left atrial enlargement (classically mitral valve disease) and P-pulmonale indicates right atrial enlargement (classically pulmonary disease / pulmonary hypertension). The P wave is best assessed in lead II and V1.

sections.heading: Key findings
items: P-mitrale (left atrial enlargement): broad (>120 ms), notched, 'M-shaped' P wave in lead II (bifid with >40 ms between peaks); a deep, broad negative terminal portion of the P wave in V1
P-pulmonale (right atrial enlargement): tall, peaked P wave >2.5 mm in the inferior leads (II, III, aVF)
Right atrial enlargement may also show a prominent initial positive deflection of the biphasic P wave in V1
Biatrial enlargement: features of both may coexist

references.label: AHA/ACCF/HRS Standardization and Interpretation of the ECG Part V: Chamber Hypertrophy (Circulation 2009)

title: Bifascicular block on ECG
summary: Bifascicular block is the combination of RBBB with block of one of the left bundle's fascicles (anterior or posterior). It indicates significant conduction system disease and, particularly with symptoms or first-degree AV block ('trifascicular' pattern), carries a risk of progression to complete heart block.

sections.heading: Key findings
items: RBBB + left anterior fascicular block: RBBB morphology with marked left axis deviation (approximately -45 to -90 degrees)
RBBB + left posterior fascicular block: RBBB morphology with right axis deviation (and other causes of right axis excluded)
Addition of first-degree AV block (prolonged PR) is sometimes termed 'trifascicular block' pattern
Left anterior fascicular block alone: left axis deviation with small q in I/aVL and small r in inferior leads, QRS <120 ms

redFlags: Bifascicular block with syncope or with intermittent advanced AV block -> high risk of progression to complete heart block; urgent cardiology assessment and consider pacing
New bifascicular block in the context of acute MI is a marker of extensive disease

references.label: 2021 ESC Guidelines on cardiac pacing and cardiac resynchronization therapy (Eur Heart J)

title: Accelerated idioventricular rhythm (AIVR)
summary: AIVR is a benign ventricular rhythm at a rate of roughly 40-120/min, classically seen as a reperfusion rhythm after successful thrombolysis or PCI in acute MI. It is usually self-limiting and well tolerated, and is not treated like VT - suppression can be harmful if it is the dominant rhythm.

sections.heading: Key findings
items: Regular broad-complex (ventricular) rhythm at a rate of approximately 40-120/min (slower than VT)
Often appears as the ventricular rate accelerates to overtake a slowing sinus rate, with fusion and capture beats at onset/offset
Commonly a reperfusion rhythm after coronary reperfusion in acute MI; also seen in cardiomyopathy and digoxin toxicity
Usually transient and haemodynamically well tolerated

redFlags: AIVR itself is usually benign and self-limiting - do not treat it as VT; avoid suppressing it if it is the only effective rhythm
If loss of AV synchrony causes haemodynamic compromise, treat the underlying cause rather than the rhythm itself

references.label: Mason JW, Hancock EW, Gettes LS. AHA/ACCF/HRS recommendations for the standardization and interpretation of the ECG: Part II. Electrocardiography diagnostic statement list. Circulation 2007;115(10):1325-1332.

title: Early repolarisation pattern on ECG
summary: Early repolarisation is a common pattern of J-point elevation and notching/slurring, often a normal variant in young, fit individuals. The main bedside task is distinguishing it from STEMI and pericarditis. A subset (early repolarisation syndrome) is associated with idiopathic VF, so the pattern is interpreted with the clinical picture.

sections.heading: Key findings
items: J-point elevation with notching or slurring of the terminal QRS, typically in the inferior and/or lateral leads
Concave-upward ST elevation, usually <2 mm, often most prominent in V2-V5
Tall, slightly asymmetric T waves; the ST/T changes are stable rather than evolving
More common in young adults, athletes and men
Distinguish from STEMI (territorial, evolving, reciprocal change) and pericarditis (diffuse with PR depression)

redFlags: Do not assume J-point elevation is benign in a patient with ischaemic symptoms - use serial ECGs, troponin and comparison with prior tracings
Inferolateral early repolarisation with unexplained syncope or a family history of sudden death -> consider early repolarisation syndrome and refer

references.label: Haïssaguerre M et al. Sudden cardiac arrest associated with early repolarization. N Engl J Med 2008;358(19):2016-2023.
Macfarlane PW et al. The Early Repolarization Pattern: A Consensus Paper. J Am Coll Cardiol 2015;66(4):470-477.

title: Ectopic beats - atrial ectopics and premature ventricular complexes
summary: Premature atrial complexes (PACs) and premature ventricular complexes (PVCs) are common, usually benign extra beats. Recognising them and distinguishing narrow (supraventricular) from broad (ventricular) ectopy is the bedside task; frequent or repetitive ventricular ectopy occasionally signals underlying disease.

sections.heading: Recognition
items: Premature atrial complex (PAC): early P wave of abnormal morphology, narrow QRS, usually followed by an incomplete compensatory pause
Premature ventricular complex (PVC): early broad QRS with no preceding P wave, abnormal/bizarre morphology, usually followed by a full compensatory pause
Patterns: bigeminy (every other beat ectopic), trigeminy (every third), couplets (two in a row), triplets, salvos
Interpolated PVC: sandwiched between two sinus beats without a compensatory pause

redFlags: Very frequent PVCs, runs of >=3 (non-sustained VT), multiform PVCs, or R-on-T phenomenon -> consider underlying structural heart disease, ischaemia or electrolyte disturbance
Ectopy in the setting of syncope, known cardiomyopathy or a family history of sudden death warrants cardiology assessment

references.label: Mason JW, Hancock EW, Gettes LS. AHA/ACCF/HRS recommendations for the standardization and interpretation of the ECG: Part II. Electrocardiography diagnostic statement list. Circulation 2007;115(10):1325-1332.

title: Dextrocardia and limb-lead misplacement
summary: An unexpected pattern of negative complexes in lead I with poor R-wave progression should prompt consideration of dextrocardia or, far more commonly, lead misplacement (especially left-right arm reversal). Recognising this prevents misdiagnosis and unnecessary investigation; the fix is to check lead placement and repeat the ECG.

sections.heading: Recognition and differentiation
items: Dextrocardia: negative P, QRS and T in lead I; inverted/reversed precordial R-wave progression (R waves get smaller from V1 to V6); right axis deviation
Left-right arm lead reversal mimics some of these limb-lead findings (inverted P/QRS in I, aVR looks like a 'normal' lead II) BUT precordial R-wave progression is normal
Key discriminator: in true dextrocardia, precordial leads also show reversed/poor R-wave progression; in arm-lead reversal, the precordial leads are normal
If dextrocardia is suspected, repeat with right-sided precordial leads (and reversed limb leads) for proper interpretation

redFlags: Always exclude lead misplacement before diagnosing dextrocardia or before acting on bizarre limb-lead findings - check electrode placement and repeat the ECG

references.label: Mason JW, Hancock EW, Gettes LS. AHA/ACCF/HRS recommendations for the standardization and interpretation of the ECG: Part II. Electrocardiography diagnostic statement list. Circulation 2007;115(10):1325-1332.
García-Niebla J et al. Technical mistakes during the acquisition of the electrocardiogram. Ann Noninvasive Electrocardiol 2009;14(4):389-403.

title: Hypomagnesaemia - causes and interpretation
summary: Low serum magnesium is common in hospitalised patients and frequently coexists with, and perpetuates, hypokalaemia and hypocalcaemia. It must be corrected to allow successful repletion of those electrolytes and to reduce arrhythmia risk, particularly torsades de pointes.

sections.heading: Causes and associations
items: Reduced intake/absorption: malnutrition, alcohol excess, malabsorption, chronic diarrhoea, proton pump inhibitors (long-term)
Renal loss: loop and thiazide diuretics, alcohol, hypercalcaemia, tubular disorders, drugs (aminoglycosides, amphotericin, cisplatin)
Refractory hypokalaemia and hypocalcaemia that will not correct until magnesium is replaced
Serum magnesium is a poor reflection of total body stores; suspect depletion clinically even with borderline levels

redFlags: Hypomagnesaemia with prolonged QT or ventricular arrhythmia (including torsades) -> give IV magnesium
Potassium that will not correct despite replacement -> check and replace magnesium

title: Hypophosphataemia - causes and interpretation
summary: Low serum phosphate impairs cellular energy (ATP) and 2,3-DPG, and when severe can cause muscle weakness (including respiratory), haemolysis and arrhythmia. A classic and dangerous context is refeeding syndrome, where insulin drives phosphate into cells.

sections.heading: Causes and mechanisms
items: Intracellular shift: refeeding syndrome, treatment of diabetic ketoacidosis (insulin), respiratory alkalosis, recovery phase of illness
Reduced intake/absorption: malnutrition, alcohol excess, chronic antacid/phosphate-binder use, vitamin D deficiency
Renal loss: hyperparathyroidism, Fanconi syndrome, diuretics, post-transplant
Severe (<0.3 mmol/L) hypophosphataemia can cause rhabdomyolysis, respiratory muscle weakness, haemolysis and arrhythmia

redFlags: Severe hypophosphataemia with respiratory muscle weakness or arrhythmia -> IV phosphate replacement
Patient at refeeding risk (prolonged starvation, alcohol excess, very low BMI) -> monitor and replace phosphate, potassium and magnesium and give thiamine before/with feeding

references.label: Merck Manual Professional - Hypophosphatemia
NICE CG32 - Nutrition support for adults (refeeding syndrome)

title: Raised alkaline phosphatase (ALP) - bone vs liver source
summary: ALP arises mainly from liver and bone, so a raised level requires identifying the source. A concurrently raised gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) points to a hepatobiliary source; an isolated raised ALP with normal GGT points to bone (or pregnancy/placenta).

sections.heading: Localising the source
items: Raised ALP with raised GGT -> hepatobiliary source (cholestasis: biliary obstruction, drugs, infiltration, primary biliary cholangitis)
Raised ALP with normal GGT -> bone source (Paget disease, osteomalacia, healing fracture, bone metastases, hyperparathyroidism) or physiological
Physiological causes of raised ALP: growing children/adolescents and the third trimester of pregnancy (placental ALP)
If unclear, ALP isoenzymes can separate bone from liver fractions

redFlags: Markedly raised ALP with jaundice and a dilated biliary tree -> biliary obstruction; arrange imaging and consider biliary sepsis
Isolated raised ALP with bone pain or hypercalcaemia -> investigate for malignancy or metabolic bone disease

references.label: Merck Manual Professional - Evaluation of the Patient With a Liver Disorder (Liver tests)

title: Abnormal TSH - interpretation algorithm
summary: TSH is the most sensitive first-line test of thyroid status in stable outpatients. Interpreting TSH with free T4 (and free T3 where relevant) classifies the disturbance as overt or subclinical hypo- or hyperthyroidism, and flags rarer central (pituitary) patterns. Acute illness distorts thyroid tests, so avoid testing in unwell inpatients unless thyroid disease is the question.

sections.heading: Interpretation pattern
items: High TSH + low free T4 -> primary hypothyroidism
High TSH + normal free T4 -> subclinical hypothyroidism
Low TSH + high free T4 (and/or free T3) -> primary hyperthyroidism
Low TSH + normal free T4 and free T3 -> subclinical hyperthyroidism
Low/normal TSH + low free T4 -> consider central (secondary) hypothyroidism or non-thyroidal illness
High TSH + high free T4 -> consider TSH-secreting adenoma, thyroid hormone resistance, or assay interference (rare)

redFlags: Suspected myxoedema coma (severe hypothyroidism with hypothermia and reduced consciousness) or thyroid storm (severe thyrotoxicosis with fever, tachyarrhythmia, agitation) -> medical emergencies
Avoid interpreting thyroid function tests during acute non-thyroidal illness (sick euthyroid pattern) unless thyroid disease is strongly suspected

references.label: Merck Manual Professional - Overview of Thyroid Function (Laboratory testing)

title: Raised creatine kinase and rhabdomyolysis
summary: Creatine kinase (CK) rises with skeletal (and cardiac) muscle injury. Rhabdomyolysis is diagnosed by a markedly elevated CK in the right clinical context and matters because myoglobin release can cause acute kidney injury, hyperkalaemia and other dangerous electrolyte shifts.

sections.heading: Interpretation
items: Rhabdomyolysis: CK typically >5 times the upper limit of normal (often quoted as >1000 U/L) with a compatible history
CK >5000 U/L is often used to define severe rhabdomyolysis; AKI risk rises with higher CK and is especially likely above ~15000-20000 U/L or with dehydration/sepsis
Causes: crush/compression injury, prolonged immobility, seizures, extreme exertion, drugs/toxins (statins, alcohol, stimulants), severe hypophosphataemia, infections
Associated findings: myoglobinuria (urine dip positive for blood with few red cells), raised potassium and phosphate, low calcium, raised urate

redFlags: Rhabdomyolysis with hyperkalaemia -> emergency; treat the potassium and protect the heart
Marked CK rise -> start aggressive IV fluid resuscitation early to prevent/limit acute kidney injury and monitor electrolytes

references.label: Merck Manual Professional - Rhabdomyolysis

title: Hyperbilirubinaemia - conjugated vs unconjugated
summary: Jaundice is classified by whether the raised bilirubin is predominantly unconjugated (pre-hepatic / impaired conjugation) or conjugated (hepatocellular or cholestatic). The split-bilirubin result, alongside the liver enzyme pattern, directs the differential and investigation.

sections.heading: Classification
items: Predominantly UNCONJUGATED (indirect) hyperbilirubinaemia: increased production (haemolysis, large haematoma resorption, ineffective erythropoiesis) or impaired conjugation (Gilbert syndrome, neonatal jaundice)
Predominantly CONJUGATED (direct) hyperbilirubinaemia: hepatocellular disease or cholestasis (intrahepatic or extrahepatic biliary obstruction)
Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia produces dark urine (bilirubinuria) and, with biliary obstruction, pale stools
Interpret with the enzyme pattern: hepatocellular (ALT/AST predominant) vs cholestatic (ALP/GGT predominant)

redFlags: Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with fever and right upper quadrant pain -> consider ascending cholangitis (a surgical/biliary emergency)
Jaundice with coagulopathy and encephalopathy -> consider acute liver failure

references.label: Merck Manual Professional - Jaundice

title: Raised serum urate (hyperuricaemia)
summary: Hyperuricaemia results from urate overproduction or underexcretion. It is associated with gout and uric acid nephrolithiasis, and a rapidly rising urate with other metabolic derangements should raise concern for tumour lysis syndrome. A normal urate during an acute attack does not exclude gout.

sections.heading: Causes and interpretation
items: Underexcretion: chronic kidney disease, diuretics (thiazides/loop), low-dose aspirin, alcohol, ciclosporin
Overproduction: high cell turnover (haematological malignancy, tumour lysis, psoriasis), purine-rich diet, fructose excess
Gout is a clinical diagnosis confirmed by joint-fluid crystals; serum urate may be normal during an acute flare, so do not exclude gout on a normal level
Markedly raised urate with raised potassium, phosphate and low calcium after chemotherapy -> consider tumour lysis syndrome

redFlags: Rapidly rising urate with hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hypocalcaemia and AKI (typically post-chemotherapy) -> tumour lysis syndrome, a medical emergency

references.label: Merck Manual Professional - Hyperuricemia and Gout

title: Low serum albumin (hypoalbuminaemia)
summary: Albumin is a negative acute-phase protein, so a low level often reflects acute illness/inflammation rather than malnutrition alone. It also affects interpretation of other tests: total calcium must be corrected for albumin, and the anion gap should be adjusted in hypoalbuminaemia.

sections.heading: Causes and interpretation
items: Reduced synthesis: chronic liver disease, malnutrition
Increased loss: nephrotic syndrome (heavy proteinuria), protein-losing enteropathy, severe burns
Redistribution/dilution: acute inflammation/sepsis (negative acute-phase response), capillary leak, fluid overload
Correct total calcium for albumin (add ~0.02 mmol/L to calcium for each 1 g/L albumin below ~40 g/L, lab-dependent), or measure ionised calcium
Correct the anion gap upward by ~2.5 mmol/L for each 10 g/L the albumin is below 40 g/L

redFlags: Low albumin with heavy proteinuria and oedema -> investigate for nephrotic syndrome
Do not act on a 'normal' total calcium in a hypoalbuminaemic patient without correcting it or checking ionised calcium

references.label: Merck Manual Professional - Hypoproteinemia / Protein metabolism overview

title: Raised ammonia and hepatic encephalopathy
summary: Ammonia is a neurotoxin normally cleared by the liver. A raised level supports hepatic encephalopathy or an inborn/acquired urea-cycle problem, but hepatic encephalopathy is primarily a clinical diagnosis - ammonia levels correlate poorly with severity and a normal level does not exclude it. Sampling artefact commonly causes falsely high results.

sections.heading: Interpretation
items: Hepatic encephalopathy is a CLINICAL diagnosis (altered mental state, asterixis, in a patient with liver disease or portosystemic shunting); ammonia supports but does not define it
Ammonia levels correlate poorly with the grade of encephalopathy; a normal level does not exclude it
Pre-analytical errors commonly cause spuriously high ammonia (delayed/warm transport, tourniquet, fist clenching) - sample on ice and process promptly
Very high ammonia without obvious chronic liver disease -> consider urea-cycle disorder, valproate toxicity or acute liver failure

redFlags: Encephalopathy with acute liver failure and rapidly rising ammonia -> risk of cerebral oedema; manage in a high-dependency/transplant-aware setting
Always look for and treat the precipitant of hepatic encephalopathy (GI bleed, infection, constipation, electrolyte disturbance, sedatives)

references.label: Merck Manual Professional - Hepatic Encephalopathy

title: Procalcitonin interpretation
summary: Procalcitonin (PCT) rises in systemic bacterial infection and is mainly used to support decisions to start and, more reliably, to stop antibiotics, rather than as a stand-alone diagnostic test. It must always be interpreted with the clinical picture; values are influenced by non-infective causes.

sections.heading: Interpretation and use
items: PCT rises within hours in significant bacterial infection and falls with effective treatment, making serial trends useful for antibiotic stewardship (especially de-escalation/stopping)
Higher values increase the probability of bacterial infection/sepsis, but no single cut-off reliably rules infection in or out
Non-infective causes of a raised PCT: major surgery/trauma, burns, cardiac arrest, severe shock, some cancers, the first days of life
A low PCT does not exclude localised infection (e.g. empyema, abscess); never withhold treatment from a clinically septic patient based on PCT alone

redFlags: Do not use procalcitonin to overrule clinical judgement - treat sepsis on clinical grounds regardless of the PCT value

references.label: NICE DG18 - Procalcitonin testing for diagnosing and monitoring sepsis

title: ESR vs CRP - interpreting the inflammatory markers
summary: CRP and ESR both rise in inflammation but with different kinetics. CRP rises and falls quickly (hours), tracking acute inflammation, whereas ESR rises and falls slowly (days-weeks) and is influenced by many non-inflammatory factors. Marked discordance can itself be informative.

sections.heading: Comparison and interpretation
items: CRP: rises within ~6-12 h, peaks ~48 h, falls quickly once inflammation resolves - good for acute monitoring
ESR: rises and falls slowly over days to weeks; influenced by age, sex, anaemia, pregnancy, and immunoglobulin/fibrinogen levels
ESR is raised non-specifically by anaemia, paraproteinaemia (e.g. myeloma) and pregnancy independent of acute inflammation
A very high ESR with a normal/low CRP -> consider paraproteinaemia (e.g. multiple myeloma) or other causes of raised plasma proteins
A markedly raised ESR is part of the assessment of suspected giant cell arteritis / polymyalgia rheumatica

redFlags: New headache or visual symptoms with a very high ESR/CRP in an older patient -> suspect giant cell arteritis; do not delay corticosteroids while awaiting biopsy

references.label: Merck Manual Professional - Acute Phase Reactants (ESR and CRP)

title: Eosinophilia - causes and interpretation
summary: Eosinophilia is an absolute eosinophil count above the normal range. The differential is broad, captured by the mnemonic of allergy/atopy, drugs, parasitic infection, connective tissue/vasculitis, and haematological/neoplastic causes. Marked or sustained eosinophilia risks end-organ damage and needs investigation.

sections.heading: Grading and causes
items: Grading: mild ~0.5-1.5, moderate ~1.5-5.0, severe >5.0 x10^9/L (hypereosinophilia is >1.5 x10^9/L)
Common causes: allergy/atopy (asthma, eczema, rhinitis), drug reactions, parasitic (helminth) infection
Less common: vasculitis (e.g. eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis), connective tissue disease, adrenal insufficiency
Haematological/neoplastic: clonal eosinophilia, myeloproliferative disorders, lymphoma, some solid tumours
Sustained hypereosinophilia can cause end-organ damage (heart, lungs, skin, nerves) - the hypereosinophilic syndromes

redFlags: Eosinophilia with fever, rash, lymphadenopathy and organ dysfunction after a new drug -> consider DRESS (drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms), a medical emergency
Marked persistent eosinophilia with cardiac or neurological involvement -> urgent haematology referral

references.label: Merck Manual Professional - Eosinophilia

title: Pancytopenia - approach and interpretation
summary: Pancytopenia is the reduction of all three cell lines (anaemia, leucopenia and thrombocytopenia). The mechanism is either reduced production (marrow failure/infiltration) or increased peripheral destruction/sequestration (e.g. hypersplenism). It can signal serious marrow disease and demands prompt evaluation, often including a blood film and marrow examination.

sections.heading: Causes and approach
items: Reduced production: aplastic anaemia, marrow infiltration (leukaemia, lymphoma, myeloma, metastases, myelofibrosis), severe B12/folate deficiency, drugs/chemotherapy, radiation
Increased destruction/sequestration: hypersplenism, severe sepsis, haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, autoimmune disease
Review the blood film for blasts, dysplasia or other clues; check B12/folate, reticulocyte count and LDH
Reticulocyte count helps separate marrow failure (low) from peripheral consumption (often higher)

redFlags: Pancytopenia with circulating blasts, or with neutropenic fever -> haematological emergency; urgent haematology referral and treat neutropenic sepsis empirically
Severe thrombocytopenia with bleeding, or symptomatic anaemia -> urgent transfusion support and investigation

references.label: Merck Manual Professional - Approach to the Patient With Cytopenias / Aplastic Anemia

title: B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP / NT-proBNP) interpretation
summary: BNP and NT-proBNP are released by stretched ventricular myocardium and are used mainly to rule OUT heart failure because of their high negative predictive value. Levels are affected by age, renal function, obesity and atrial fibrillation, so they are interpreted alongside echocardiography and the clinical picture.

sections.heading: Thresholds and interpretation
items: Acute setting (suspected acute heart failure): a low value makes heart failure unlikely - common rule-out cut-offs are BNP <100 pg/mL and NT-proBNP <300 pg/mL
Chronic/non-acute (referral) setting: NICE uses BNP >=100 pg/mL or NT-proBNP >=400 pg/mL to prompt echocardiography; ESC uses lower thresholds (BNP >=35, NT-proBNP >=125 pg/mL)
Levels rise with age, renal impairment, atrial fibrillation, sepsis and right heart strain
Levels are LOWER (falsely reassuring) in obesity and may be lowered by treatment such as sacubitril/valsartan (affects NT-proBNP and BNP differently)
Natriuretic peptides support but do not replace echocardiography for diagnosing heart failure

redFlags: Markedly raised natriuretic peptide with breathlessness -> assess urgently for decompensated heart failure (and other causes of raised levels such as PE)
Do not exclude heart failure on a borderline level in an obese patient - levels are attenuated

references.label: NICE NG106 - Chronic heart failure in adults: diagnosis and management (natriuretic peptide thresholds)
2021 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of acute and chronic heart failure (Eur Heart J)

title: Imaging for suspected acute aortic dissection
summary: Acute aortic dissection is a time-critical emergency. In a haemodynamically stable patient, ECG-gated CT angiography of the whole aorta is the first-line investigation because it is fast, widely available and accurate. Transoesophageal echocardiography or MRI are alternatives depending on stability and local expertise.

sections.heading: Modality selection
items: Stable patient with suspected acute aortic syndrome -> CT angiography of the chest, abdomen and pelvis (whole aorta) is first-line
Unstable patient who cannot be moved to CT -> bedside transoesophageal echocardiography (TOE) is the alternative
MRI is highly accurate but is generally reserved for stable patients and follow-up due to availability and acquisition time
A normal D-dimer may help lower probability in low-risk patients but does not replace imaging where clinical suspicion is significant
A normal chest X-ray (e.g. no widened mediastinum) does NOT exclude dissection

redFlags: Sudden severe tearing chest/back pain with pulse or blood-pressure differential, new aortic regurgitation, or malperfusion -> arrange immediate aortic imaging and involve cardiothoracic surgery
Do not delay definitive imaging for a normal chest X-ray or D-dimer if clinical suspicion is high

references.label: 2014 ESC Guidelines on the diagnosis and treatment of aortic diseases (Eur Heart J)

title: Imaging for suspected cauda equina syndrome
summary: Cauda equina syndrome is a surgical emergency. When red flags are present, an urgent MRI of the whole spine (lumbosacral, ideally whole spine) is the definitive investigation and should be obtained emergently - including out of hours - so that decompression can occur as soon as safely possible.

sections.heading: Red flags and imaging
items: Red flags: bilateral sciatica, saddle (perineal) anaesthesia, bladder or bowel dysfunction (urinary retention or incontinence, faecal incontinence), reduced anal tone, and severe or progressive bilateral neurological deficit
Suspected cauda equina syndrome -> EMERGENCY MRI of the spine, available at the admitting hospital and out of hours
MRI is the definitive test; do not rely on plain films or CT, which can miss the diagnosis
If MRI is contraindicated or unavailable, urgent transfer/discussion with the spinal/neurosurgical service is required - CT myelography is an alternative

redFlags: New urinary retention, saddle anaesthesia or bilateral leg symptoms with back pain -> emergency MRI and immediate neurosurgical/spinal referral; delay risks permanent bladder, bowel and sexual dysfunction

references.label: NICE CKS - Sciatica (lumbar radiculopathy): cauda equina red flags

title: Imaging for first-trimester vaginal bleeding
summary: In early pregnancy with bleeding or pain, the priority is to exclude ectopic pregnancy. Pelvic (transvaginal) ultrasound, interpreted alongside serum beta-hCG, is the first-line investigation to locate the pregnancy and assess viability. A pregnancy of unknown location requires careful follow-up.

sections.heading: Approach
items: First-line imaging: transvaginal pelvic ultrasound to determine pregnancy location (intrauterine vs extrauterine) and viability
Interpret ultrasound with serum beta-hCG; above the discriminatory zone an intrauterine pregnancy is usually visible if present
No intrauterine pregnancy on scan with a positive hCG = 'pregnancy of unknown location' -> follow up with serial hCG and repeat scan via an early pregnancy assessment service
Free fluid in the pelvis with an empty uterus and a positive pregnancy test is highly concerning for ectopic

redFlags: Haemodynamic instability with a positive pregnancy test -> suspect ruptured ectopic pregnancy; resuscitate and arrange emergency gynaecology/surgical input - do not delay for imaging
Significant pain or adnexal mass with free fluid -> urgent gynaecology referral

references.label: NICE NG126 - Ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage: diagnosis and initial management

title: Imaging for suspected deep vein thrombosis (DVT)
summary: Suspected lower-limb DVT is investigated using the two-level Wells score to stratify risk, combined with D-dimer and proximal leg vein ultrasound (Doppler). The pathway avoids unnecessary imaging in low-probability patients with a negative D-dimer.

sections.heading: Two-level Wells pathway (NICE)
items: Calculate the two-level DVT Wells score: 'DVT likely' = 2 points or more; 'DVT unlikely' = 1 point or less
DVT likely (>=2): offer a proximal leg vein ultrasound, ideally within 4 hours; if it cannot be done within 4 hours, give interim anticoagulation, do a D-dimer, and scan within 24 hours
If the proximal ultrasound is negative but the D-dimer is positive in a 'likely' patient, repeat the ultrasound 6-8 days later
DVT unlikely (<=1): perform a D-dimer; if negative, DVT is excluded; if positive, proceed to proximal leg vein ultrasound (within 4 hours, or anticoagulate and scan within 24 hours)

redFlags: Signs of associated pulmonary embolism (breathlessness, chest pain, hypoxia, tachycardia) -> investigate for PE in parallel
Phlegmasia (massive proximal DVT with a swollen, painful, discoloured limb and threatened limb viability) -> emergency vascular input

references.label: NICE NG158 - Venous thromboembolic diseases: diagnosis, management and thrombophilia testing

title: Imaging for paediatric head injury (PECARN)
summary: The PECARN rule identifies children at very low risk of clinically important traumatic brain injury (ciTBI) after minor head trauma, in whom CT can be safely avoided. It uses age-specific (under 2 years and 2 years and older) predictors. The rule is unidirectional: meeting no criteria allows CT to be avoided, but meeting a criterion does not mandate CT.

sections.heading: PECARN predictors by age group
items: Under 2 years: GCS <15 or other signs of altered mental status, palpable skull fracture, loss of consciousness >=5 seconds, non-frontal (occipital/parietal/temporal) scalp haematoma, severe mechanism of injury, or acting abnormally per parent
2 years and older: GCS <15 or other signs of altered mental status, signs of basilar skull fracture, history of loss of consciousness, vomiting, severe mechanism of injury, or severe headache

Severe mechanism: high-speed road traffic collision (ejection, death of another occupant, rollover), pedestrian/cyclist without helmet struck by a vehicle, fall >0.9 m (under 2 years) or >1.5 m (2 years and older), or head struck by a high-impact object

Highest-risk features (GCS <15, altered mental status, palpable skull fracture under 2 / signs of basilar skull fracture 2+) -> CT recommended; lower-risk features -> CT vs observation, using clinician experience, multiple findings, worsening, age <3 months and parental preference

redFlags: GCS <15, focal neurology, suspected open/depressed or basilar skull fracture, post-traumatic seizure or worsening symptoms -> urgent CT head
PECARN is a guide for very-low-risk identification, not a substitute for serial clinical assessment; also use the local national guideline (e.g. NICE NG232 in the UK)

references.label: Kuppermann N et al. PECARN - Identification of children at very low risk of clinically-important brain injuries (Lancet 2009)

title: Skeletal survey for suspected non-accidental injury (NAI)
summary: When physical abuse is suspected, a full skeletal survey is the standard imaging to detect occult and healing fractures. It is mandatory in children under 2 years (and in older children with poor verbal ability/developmental delay). It is a structured set of individual radiographs - never a single whole-body 'babygram'.

sections.heading: Principles
items: Indicated when physical abuse is suspected, and is mandatory in children under 2 years of age (and in older children unable to reliably report injury)
A full skeletal survey is a defined series of dedicated, separately coned radiographs covering the whole skeleton - a single whole-body 'babygram' is not acceptable
Performed by trained radiographers and reported by radiologists with relevant expertise; CT head is added where intracranial injury is suspected
A follow-up limited skeletal survey is recommended approximately 11-14 days later to detect healing fractures not initially visible

redFlags: Suspected physical abuse is a safeguarding emergency -> involve the safeguarding/child protection team and senior paediatrician immediately, alongside imaging
Certain fractures (e.g. metaphyseal corner, posterior rib, multiple fractures of differing ages) are strongly associated with abuse and require expert review

references.label: Royal College of Radiologists / RCPCH - The radiological investigation of suspected physical abuse in children (2018)

title: Imaging for biliary colic and suspected cholecystitis
summary: For right-upper-quadrant pain suggestive of gallstone disease, abdominal ultrasound is the first-line investigation. It is widely available, radiation-free, and reliably detects gallstones and signs of cholecystitis. It also identifies biliary dilatation that may indicate ductal obstruction.

sections.heading: Approach
items: First-line imaging: right upper quadrant / abdominal ultrasound to look for gallstones, gallbladder wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid and a sonographic Murphy sign (cholecystitis)
Ultrasound also assesses the common bile duct calibre - dilatation suggests ductal stones/obstruction
If ductal stones are suspected (dilated duct, deranged liver tests) -> MRCP (or endoscopic ultrasound) to image the biliary tree
If ultrasound is equivocal for acute cholecystitis -> consider further imaging (CT, MRI, or cholescintigraphy); in pregnancy, MRI is the preferred second-line test

redFlags: Right upper quadrant pain with fever and jaundice (Charcot triad) -> suspect ascending cholangitis; arrange urgent imaging and biliary drainage
Signs of severe/complicated cholecystitis (gangrene, perforation, sepsis) -> urgent surgical referral

references.label: ACR Appropriateness Criteria - Right Upper Quadrant Pain (2022 Update)

title: Imaging for suspected pulmonary tuberculosis
summary: A chest X-ray is the key initial imaging test in suspected active pulmonary tuberculosis and helps prioritise infection control and microbiological sampling. Imaging supports but never replaces microbiological confirmation (sputum smear, culture and nucleic acid amplification testing).

sections.heading: Approach
items: First-line imaging: posteroanterior chest X-ray when active pulmonary TB is suspected
Classic (reactivation) findings: upper-lobe or apical consolidation, cavitation, fibronodular change, and lymphadenopathy; miliary TB shows diffuse fine nodules
Imaging is supportive - send respiratory samples for smear, culture and rapid molecular testing (e.g. nucleic acid amplification) to confirm and assess drug resistance
CT may clarify equivocal X-ray findings or complications; a normal chest X-ray makes active pulmonary TB unlikely but does not exclude it in immunocompromised patients

redFlags: Suspected infectious pulmonary TB (cough, weight loss, night sweats, haemoptysis, cavitation) -> institute airborne infection control (respiratory isolation) immediately while investigating
Notify public health and screen contacts when TB is confirmed or strongly suspected

references.label: NICE NG33 - Tuberculosis: diagnosis and management
WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis: systematic screening (chest radiography)

title: Contrast-associated AKI and the eGFR threshold for iodinated contrast
summary: Iodinated contrast for CT carries a small risk of contrast-associated acute kidney injury (CA-AKI), concentrated in patients with significantly reduced renal function. Current ACR/NKF guidance reassures that the risk in patients with an eGFR at or above 30 mL/min/1.73 m2 is low, so contrast should not be unduly withheld when the scan is clinically important.

sections.heading: Risk and thresholds
items: Patients with eGFR >=30 mL/min/1.73 m2 (and no acute kidney injury) are at low risk of CA-AKI from intravenous iodinated contrast
Patients with eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m2, or with acute kidney injury, are the higher-risk group requiring individualised assessment and consideration of prophylactic IV fluids
Weigh the risk of withholding a clinically necessary contrast study (delayed/missed diagnosis) against a generally small and often reversible AKI risk

Metformin: in patients with eGFR >=30 and no AKI, metformin does not need to be stopped before IV iodinated contrast and no post-contrast renal check is needed; review/withhold below this threshold or with AKI
Use the patient's clinical condition: AKI, dehydration and nephrotoxins increase risk independent of baseline eGFR

redFlags: Do not withhold time-critical contrast-enhanced imaging (e.g. suspected aortic dissection, major trauma, stroke thrombectomy work-up) for renal-function concerns alone - the diagnostic benefit usually outweighs the risk

references.label: ACR / National Kidney Foundation Consensus Statements - Use of Intravenous Iodinated Contrast Media in Patients with Kidney Disease (Radiology 2020)

title: MRI safety - contraindications and screening
summary: MRI uses a powerful static magnetic field and radiofrequency energy, creating hazards from ferromagnetic objects, certain implants and projectiles. Rigorous safety screening before every scan is essential. Many modern implants are MR-conditional, but each must be verified against its labelling before scanning.

sections.heading: Key safety considerations
items: Screen for implanted electronic/active devices: pacemakers, implantable defibrillators, neurostimulators, cochlear implants, programmable shunts and infusion pumps - scan only if confirmed MR-conditional and per protocol
Ferromagnetic hazards: intraocular/intracranial metallic foreign bodies, certain aneurysm clips, some older implants, and loose ferromagnetic objects that can become projectiles
Ask about recent surgery/implants and obtain device documentation; many implants are MR-conditional but require specific field strength and scanning conditions
Gadolinium contrast: use with caution in severe renal impairment (risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis with older agents); avoid unnecessary use in pregnancy
Remove all ferromagnetic objects; the static field is always on even when not scanning

redFlags: Never take a patient or unscreened equipment into the MRI scanner room without completing safety screening - projectile and device hazards can be fatal
Suspected metallic intraocular foreign body (e.g. previous grinding/metalwork injury) -> screen (e.g. orbital X-ray) before MRI

references.label: ACR Manual on MR Safety (American College of Radiology)
